# Ridgeway Service and Reference Decision Record

As Ridgeway 3.4 was being wrapped up, server placeholder visibility and inline reference depth were added to this record together. Both came up in the same cleanup pass and initially pointed people back to the service object; this only shows that the investigation entry points overlapped at the time, not that the same logic already handled both.

The earliest local location recorded was:

`packages/elements-core/src/__fixtures__/services/with-url-variables.ts`

The filename points to a service fixture with a URL variable. The direct dependency visible at the top of the file is:

```ts
import { IHttpService } from '@stoplight/types';
```

These two details point back to the service material, but don't tell us what the page displays. Having a variable in the fixture doesn't mean the placeholder content in template URL remains recognizable when displayed; the type import only shows that the file directly uses a service type name.

The initial draft had two possible directions. One was to group both issues under "incomplete service definition display" and keep investigating from their shared entry point. The other was to keep the two issue names: on the service template side, keep looking for the placeholder portion and variable-related information in URL; on the reference side, look separately for objects whose levels can be compared. We'll use the latter wording here for now.

This isn't because we can already separate implementation responsibilities, but because the samples we're missing are different. The service template side needs to establish whether users see the template itself, the substituted address, or something other than either. For inline reference depth, we need the levels of the reference relationships and where they stop. Nested fields in a service object do not automatically constitute a reference chain; a reference appearing in a piece of page content does not automatically show that it has been expanded to a given depth.

Keep this as a working assumption: starting from the service fixture with a URL variable may help us revisit both lines of investigation. It only sets the search order; it isn't a common conclusion.

Still needed: when template URL is displayed, where the placeholder portion and the accompanying variable information each end up; what object to use for comparing levels in inline reference depth.

# Ridgeway Service and Reference Decision Record

This page originally recorded server placeholder visibility and inline reference depth side by side. After review, we kept their shared history but withdrew the interpretation that "one service object can establish both points." Both were raised in the same closeout round for Ridgeway 3.4; that does not mean they share a confirmed display path.

## Service materials remain the earliest entry point

The earliest recorded object has not changed:

`packages/elements-core/src/__fixtures__/services/with-url-variables.ts`

This is a service fixture path with a URL variable. The file header contains:

```ts
import { IHttpService } from '@stoplight/types';
```

These two items are useful for local navigation. Readers can use the service fixture, the URL variable, and `IHttpService` to revisit the existing materials. They do not directly describe what remains on the page, nor do they explain where references continue or stop. The first draft put "finding a service fixture with a variable" too close to "confirming that the user sees template content," making it easy to mistake the path for a display result; those points are now kept separate.

The service-template side is missing an observation of what is displayed. We need to distinguish the placeholder portion of template URL, the information attached to the variable, and any literal address that may ultimately appear. Confirming only that the object contains a variable does not tell us whether this content is still included in what is displayed.

The reference side is missing a comparison of levels. Field structure, object nesting, or a segment of embedded content cannot establish inline reference depth on its own. At a minimum, we need to distinguish the reference object, the content that continues to expand, and where expansion stops before the material can be recorded as depth-related.

## The combined sequence used earlier

Early troubleshooting tried a convenient sequence: first confirm that the service object can be read; if the page content looks incomplete, check placeholder content and reference expansion together. This sequence has not been removed because it explains why earlier searches associated both issue names with the service fixture.

But "one inspection" must not become "one result explains both." If the service address contains a variable and the page shows only the substituted literal address, then "the fixture contains a variable" and "the placeholder content is still identifiable" are clearly not the same thing. Conversely, if the page shows only a segment of reference content with no second-level object for comparison, then "a reference appears on the page" and "the reference depth has been established" are not the same thing either.

These two narrow counterexamples provide no new attribution of implementation responsibility and supply no level count. They change only how we record things: new material must first state whether it addresses template URL and variable information, or the expansion boundary of the reference relationship; "complete service display" can no longer be used as an umbrella term for both issues.

## Findings retained after review

The review could still confirm only a few things directly: the service fixture path with the URL variable exists, the file header contains a `IHttpService` import, and this is a starting point for finding further service-side material. No direct snippet was retained alongside it that could map the variable content to the user-visible result, and no inline reference chain suitable for comparison appeared.

The shared entry point has therefore been scaled back from a potential line of proof to a historical search lead. The path is worth keeping because it explains why the investigation started with service materials; it does not explain what is responsible for display or where references are handled. `IHttpService` is only the name of a type directly used by that fixture file, nothing more.

There was another misreading on the reference side: because the service object with a variable had several structural levels, it was treated as a sample for inline reference depth. The review did not accept this. A variable may reside in URL or in the service object's structure, but apparent nesting is not a reference relationship. Without an explicit reference object and comparable levels, we cannot infer "depth has been covered" from "it looks nested."

The reverse inference does not hold either. Even if one level of reference content is observed later, that does not establish that the placeholder portion of template URL and the variable information are still retained. The two may appear next to each other during a single browsing session, but neither can serve as a sample for the other.

## Review addendum

The review did not ask for the page to be split into two unrelated records. The shared history is still useful: it preserves why the two issues entered the Ridgeway 3.4 closeout together, as well as the earliest entry point into the service materials. What the review pared back was the overly broad inference.

The short margin note reads:

> An entry point is not a sample.
>
> Whether placeholder content is still present and how many levels a reference reaches should each be recorded with the relevant material.
>
> Without a comparison of levels, do not fill in a number for the reference side.

The decision is to continue using one shared-history record while maintaining two lines of assessment. The service-template side will use the fixture with the URL variable to revisit template URL and variable-related content; inline reference depth awaits reference samples that show differences between levels. If the same object does later turn out to involve both sides, document what it establishes for each line separately.

Two items have yet to be added: the result users see when the service template is actually displayed, and comparison samples for reference depth. Keeping them on the same page has not merged them into a single to-do.

# Ridgeway Service and Reference Decision Record

After several additions to this record, what remains is not a straight line from requirements to implementation, but a set of judgments that have been narrowed down. server placeholder visibility and inline reference depth were first written down side by side, then someone added the service fixture entry point, someone crossed out the broad term "service display", and someone asked to retain the old terminology, so that later searches would not lump different phenomena back into the same conclusion.

The shared page is still retained. It preserves why the two issues converged as Ridgeway 3.4 was being wrapped up, and why the early investigation first focused on service objects. It does not describe this convergence as a shared implementation, nor does it present a single service artifact as substitute evidence for the two behaviors.

The paragraphs below are retained in the order in which they were recorded at the time. Earlier paragraphs support only the judgments that were justified at the time; later corrections are not retroactively written back into the original notes.

## 2023-05-24: The Initial Two Threads

The earliest notes named two issues that had not yet been resolved: server placeholder visibility and inline reference depth. At the time, both were mixed together with "whether the content is complete after opening a service definition". This broad term was convenient, but did not specify whether the content in question was template URL, information attached to variables, object structure, or embedded reference content.

The most stable local object in the initial notes was:

`packages/elements-core/src/__fixtures__/services/with-url-variables.ts`

The filename led the investigation first to a service fixture with a URL variable. The file header shows:

```ts
import { IHttpService } from '@stoplight/types';
```

The record stopped here at the time. The path explains why the investigation first looked for service materials; the import shows that the file directly uses `IHttpService`. Neither provides the URL that the user actually saw, nor a reference relationship that can be compared layer by layer.

The initial draft proposed two options. The first was to continue combining the two issues as "incomplete service definition display", find a common entry point and then fill in the details. The second was to continue keeping their histories on the same page, but look for different samples separately: on the service template side examine template URL and variable-related content, and on the reference side examine reference relationships, visible levels and stopping points.

At the time, we chose the second option, not because we already knew who was responsible for each side, but because the missing pieces were different. The presence of variable in a service fixture does not show that the user can still distinguish the placeholders in the template. An object appearing to have several field levels does not establish that those levels are inline reference. At the end of the initial draft, only a weaker working judgment remained: a service fixture with the URL variable might serve as the starting point for continuing to look back along both tracks.

This judgment was later often misread as meaning that "the shared entry point had been confirmed." The original meaning was not that strong. It only said that, at the time, both issues began by looking near the service object; it did not say that the same file could provide a conclusion for both sides.

## Early Retained Legacy Approach

After the initial draft, the page once used a convenient working sequence. The original text is retained below:

> Enter through a service fixture with variables, first confirm that the service object can be read; when page content is incomplete, check the placeholder content and reference expansion at the same time, then use the same result to update both items.

This section is now marked as deprecated, but it is not deleted. Older searches often reached this page through "service display" or "incomplete content"; removing the original sentence would instead leave readers unsure why the template URL and the reference hierarchy were once considered together.

The first half of the legacy approach was not entirely useless. Starting from a service fixture with variables remains a local entry point into the service materials. The problem lies specifically in "checking simultaneously" and "updating both with the same result." Being able to read the service object does not mean that the placeholder content in template URL is still within the display scope; a page address that appears readable does not mean that variable metadata is still retained. Conversely, the appearance of a piece of reference content on the page does not mean that the reference has been expanded to a level that can be assessed.

This legacy approach also treated "incomplete page content" as a single phenomenon. Only later review showed that this phrase could refer to at least three different situations: the template being replaced with a literal address, information accompanying the variable not being in a user-visible location, or a piece of reference content not being expanded further. All three situations can make the content seem incomplete, but they cannot be handled with the same object or the same conclusion.

The reason for retaining this legacy approach is not to continue recommending it, but to show where the later split began. It once caused a narrow service-side investigation to be written up as if both tracks had produced results.

## 2024-01-04: Revisiting the Service Fixture

The review draft returned to `packages/elements-core/src/__fixtures__/services/with-url-variables.ts`. What can be reconfirmed this time is still only a local fact: the path points to a service fixture with the URL variable, the file header contains an `IHttpService` import, and the service-template side can continue the review from here.

The review yielded no new page snippets. None of the material could directly map the variable in the fixture to the service display seen by users, and there was no explicit reference chain available for comparison. As a result, this review did not elevate "the variable exists" to "placeholder content is visible", nor did it elevate the object structure to "reference depth is confirmed".

An overly hasty inference had been made here: since the search terms for both issues led to material related to services, the service object could be used as a common sample to consolidate the shared page. The review did not accept this. The object identification was supportable, but the behavioral conclusions did not follow. The shared entry point was scaled back from a potential avenue for proof to a historical search direction.

The same review also exposed a terminology issue. Someone had called the levels within the service object inline reference depth. That wording was not retained. Variables may exist in URL or in the service object structure; nesting in a structure does not mean that it contains a reference relationship. Without an explicit reference object, readers cannot tell whether a given level is the object itself, variable metadata, or an embedded result, much less where processing stops.

The reverse substitution is not valid either. Even if a page later shows one level of embedded content, that cannot answer, for the service template side, whether the placeholder portion and variable information are retained or removed. The two issues may be discussed in adjacent areas of a page, but appearing together does not mean they prove each other.

## Revisions in the Review Margins

After the review, this page was not split into two isolated documents. The shared history was still useful in its own right: it explained why the two issues were raised side by side as Ridgeway 3.4 was being wrapped up, and why the earliest search started with a service fixture containing a URL variable.

The review changed the narrative order. Paths, required samples, and supportable decisions must be written up separately. Previously, readers saw "service display" first, followed by the URL variable, fixtures, references, and page content, making it easy to read these terms as an already verified processing chain.

The margin notes left at the time were:

> An entry point is not a sample.
>
> Whether placeholder content remains and how many levels references traverse should not be combined into a single acceptance statement.
>
> Without a level-by-level comparison, do not fill in numbers for the reference side.

These notes added no implementation information. They recorded an explicit rejection: file paths cannot substitute for observations of the display, and general nesting cannot substitute for reference levels.

The review also preserved the significance of the service fixture. It had not been proven irrelevant, but was instead returned to a narrower role: local navigation on the service template side. `IHttpService` was likewise treated only as the type name used directly by the file. Neither was any longer treated as an explanation of display responsibilities, reference responsibilities, or page results.

The limited-scope decision reached at this stage was: the shared page would remain; new material must specify whether it addresses service templates or reference levels; when material is added to only one side, the results must not casually be written into the other side just because the title still lists both.

## A Follow-up Check That Did Not Produce a Consolidated Result

The follow-up check after the review did not re-enable the old approach. The fact that the service object can be read still does not resolve the question of "which parts of template URL can be identified." The reference side also did not obtain a sample that clearly distinguishes further expansion, visible levels, and the stopping point.

The value of this follow-up check is that it made the old umbrella term even less tenable. Previously, "incomplete service-definition display" sounded like a single, unified problem, but in practice it made different pieces of material stand in for one another. A service object containing variable would be used in place of a reference chain; an embedded piece of content, in turn, would be used in place of the display result for template URL.

Later, the page stopped using the wording "one result updates two items." If a piece of material only describes the service object's path, fixture name, or type adjacency, record it only up to the point of locating the object. If a piece of material only indicates that there is a segment of referenced content, first record whether it is actually a reference object, and only then discuss hierarchy. This change did not solve the two problems, but it prevented the record from continuing to expand into unconfirmed areas.

At this stage, another abandoned phrase was "address complete." It made it easy to conflate the apparent readability of a literal address with the continued retention of the template structure. On the service-template side, these two observations need not be the same: an address can be readable even though the placeholder parts in the template are no longer identifiable; conversely, retaining the template structure does not mean that all address conditions have been verified.

This follow-up check also did not produce a new assignment of responsibility. The page only laid out the known objects, the missing observations, and the two threads that were still kept separate. Where there is no new fragment, the gap remains blank; do not use the old path to fill in a result.

## Outdated Operation Still Left in Place

The passage below was once treated as a practical lookup instruction and is now retained as a historical record:

> First check whether the service object exists, then check whether the page has content; if both sides have content, you can consider the service display closed out.

This passage is no longer applicable. "Service object exists" is about locating the object; "whether the page has content" does not specify what the content is. They do not distinguish among the template URL, placeholder parts, variable metadata, and reference relationships. Linking the two sentences only makes "closure" appear broader than the material actually in hand.

The old prompt was retained because it once influenced the subsequent reading order. After entering through the service object, some people would go straight to looking for an overall page status, and as a result treat the URL variable and inline references as the same category of missing item. Now, first determine which thread the material at hand belongs to, then decide whether it is worth extrapolating further.

For the service-template thread, the file path can still serve as an entry point for review; it no longer carries a guarantee of "page completeness." For the reference thread, the path is neither a confirmed reference sample nor a decision point for expansion depth. This distinction does not invalidate the old entry point; it merely limits what it can establish.

An unfinished note also remains next to the old operation: "If only the replaced address remains on the page, check further……" There is no object name or result after it. It cannot be filled in as the current step, but it can indicate that, at the time, attention had already been drawn to a possible difference between the literal address and the template display.

## 2025-04-01: Correcting the earlier interpretation on the service-template side

What the latest addendum needs to correct is not "starting the search from the service fixture", but the idea of treating the literal address after variable substitution as the only display output. Earlier notes implicitly assumed that as long as the final address looked usable, the service display was complete. That judgment was too narrow.

The service-template side must now distinguish between two kinds of objects: the placeholder portions in template URL, and the metadata attached to variables. They are not optional background in service fixtures, nor may they be omitted when interpolation is disabled just because the address is still readable. The previously recorded paths and imports are still useful, but only for retrieving service materials related to the URL variable.

The current requirement is as follows:

The getServersToDisplay server display preserves templated URL placeholders and variable metadata when interpolation is disabled.

This requirement only covers the service-template track of server display. It makes clear that when interpolation is disabled, templated URL placeholders and variable metadata must still be preserved. Earlier statements such as "the fixture contains variables" and "the service object can be read" as well as "the address looks complete" are all insufficient substitutes for this requirement, because they do not specify both the condition and the objects to be preserved.

This is also a direct correction to the old approach. Disabling interpolation is not permission to flatten the template structure into a literal address. When service-side materials are added to this page, they should focus on whether the placeholder portions of template URL and variable metadata are still preserved by server display, rather than treating address readability alone as the completion criterion.

This requirement does not extend to inline reference depth. It does not specify how many levels of references should be expanded, does not state where the reference chain stops, and does not turn service fixtures with the URL variable into examples of reference expansion. What the shared page preserves is the historical relationship, not a merging of behaviors.

To prevent later readers from interpreting the current position as an implementation workflow again, the evolution diagram shows only object relationships and branches that are still open:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Service fixture entry point" as FixtureEntry
    state "Two issue tracks" as TwoLines
    state "Service template track" as ServiceTemplate
    state "Reference hierarchy track" as ReferenceDepth
    state "Current service display requirements" as CurrentDisplayRule
    state "Hierarchy samples still needed" as SamplePending

    [*] --> FixtureEntry
    FixtureEntry --> TwoLines
    TwoLines --> ServiceTemplate
    TwoLines --> ReferenceDepth
    ServiceTemplate --> CurrentDisplayRule
    ReferenceDepth --> SamplePending
    CurrentDisplayRule --> [*]
```

The "Service fixture entry point" in the diagram corresponds only to the recorded paths and type imports. "Two issue tracks" means that they are recorded side by side in the same history, not that they share an implementation. "Hierarchy samples still needed" preserves the unresolved status of the reference side; it is not a newly invented processing node.

## inline reference depth remains unresolved

The reference track remains at the limits of the available material. The current open question is not an abstract question of "whether references go deep enough", but that the unit of documentation has not yet been determined: should subsequent samples be described in terms of reference chains, embedded content visible on the page, or the embedded objects themselves.

The existing material provides no examples that would allow a choice among these units. Until reference material with at least two comparable levels is available, this page will not add a seemingly precise number of levels, nor will it treat arbitrary nested structures as inline reference. Neither the variable structure in a service object nor a standalone piece of content on a page is sufficient to support this conclusion.

If a reference example that also passes through a service object appears in the future, the record should be split into two sentences: what it tells us about the template URL and variable metadata; what it tells us about the visible levels of the reference and where it stops. One object can provide material for both tracks separately, but its appearance on the same page does not automatically answer both questions.

This unresolved item remains on this page so that people arriving through the old issue name know: the service-template track already has clear requirements, and the reference track has not been assumed complete simply because the title places them side by side. Keeping it in its original location makes it easier to connect to real examples in the future than reusing "service display completeness".

A related question also remains here: if the referenced content itself comes from a service object with a URL variable, the page should first record what it is displayed as, then record whether it constitutes a reference relationship. These two steps cannot be compressed into "the service object has nesting". There is currently no corresponding fragment from a real page, so this question remains only in the record.

## Review and meeting excerpts

One review left the following summary:

> The shared history can be retained, but a shared entry point must not be treated as shared responsibility. Find separate examples for template preservation and reference expansion; do not fill gaps in a track that has no examples with results from the other track.

Another meeting margin note was shorter:

> First ask "what does this material show", then ask "which track can it support".

These two excerpts explain why the page has not been organized into a unified set of display rules. They do not add any new API or page behavior, nor do they expand the review comments into requirements for all service documents.

Two decisions were retained after the review. First, the shared history will remain on a single page, because the convergence of the two issues and the old search path are themselves worth tracing. Second, the service-template side and the reference side must accumulate material separately; new facts on one track do not automatically change the status of the other.

## Retained old examples

### Old example one: Recording the presence of a variable as a display result

Early notes once abbreviated "the fixture contains a URL variable" as "the placeholder content will be displayed". This shorthand was later corrected, but remains in the appendix. It explains why the initial investigation relied too heavily on file entry points: the presence of a variable in an object does indeed make it easy to jump to the conclusion that the variable will still be displayed on the page.

When encountering that path, service object, or `IHttpService` now, first treat them as information for locating the relevant material. Only when the material covers both the state of interpolation and the preservation of template placeholder content and variable metadata by server display should it be used to assess service-template behavior. The earliest note did not include these points, so it retains its less definitive historical assessment rather than being rewritten as today's requirements.

### Old example two: Recording apparent nesting as reference depth

Another old interpretation was that the appearance of a nested structure on a page or in an object meant that inline reference depth was already covered. This assessment no longer applies either. Nesting may come from a service object, a variable structure, or the page layout; it does not in itself constitute a reference chain, nor can it tell readers where expansion ends.

The earlier examples remain because "nesting" and "references" can easily appear side by side in search results. When the word nesting appears, first identify the actual reference relationship, then determine whether there are comparable levels. Without a sample, leaving the question open is more accurate than inventing a depth.

### Earlier Example Three: Treating a Shared Entry Point as Shared Responsibility

There is another, less conspicuous earlier usage: because both issues had previously been approached through the same fixture path, that path was treated as a shared point of responsibility for the two features. This usage was not accepted. File paths and direct imports can support local navigation, but they cannot be used to determine who is responsible for template display, reference processing, or page output.

The path therefore still appears on this page, but only in the context of verifying service templates. It is no longer depicted as a central node that can yield conclusions for both lines of inquiry. The old umbrella term can explain the history, but it cannot replace the current assessment.

### Earlier Example Four: Treating a Single Browsing Session as a Result

Earlier records also treated "seeing service information and reference content together on the same page" as meaning that both issues already had results. This example has no corresponding page screenshot or call snippet, so only the error in judgment itself is retained, without reconstructing the display order. Appearing alongside each other only indicates adjacency along the browsing path; it does not indicate behavioral continuity between the two objects.

## Items Left in the Margins

The service-template line of inquiry already has clear requirements. Any subsequent material added to this page should focus on whether template placeholder content and variable metadata are retained when interpolation is disabled, rather than using "the object is readable", "variables exist", or "the address is fine" as shorthand for this.

The reference side still needs an object that can show differences in levels. Before the material arrives, first clarify whether it records a reference chain, embedded content visible on the page, or the embedded object; only then discuss further expansion and where to stop. The service fixture does not automatically become a sample for this line of inquiry just because its name contains variables.

The final decisions retained in this record have three layers: the two issues will continue to share a page to preserve their common history; service templates will be handled according to the server display requirements above; inline reference depth remains a separate investigation and will not be replaced by service variables or general nesting structures. Earlier operations, review side notes, and misreadings in the appendix remain here because they show which inferences had been made and why they were later narrowed.

versions.body:
# Ridgeway Server Interpolation Proposal

This review of Ridgeway 3.4 considers default server interpolation and tablet responsive breakpoint in the same round, but the implementation of each should be assessed separately. The former concerns how the server template is displayed; the latter should cover only presentation at tablet widths.

The initial draft leans toward a conservative approach: when displaying URL, retain the server variable template text rather than substituting default values in the UI layer. This lets users see the original variable positions, at the cost of a less immediately readable default server address. The tablet responsive breakpoint will initially be treated as a separate candidate, without using the breakpoint to rewrite the currently selected server.

The tentative starting point for investigation is `packages/elements-core/src/hooks/useChosenServerUrl.ts`. Confirm when the default server is selected along this path before deciding whether interpolation should happen before display.

Withdrawal conditions: if substituting default values would affect non-default server selection, or if the tablet layout would also change server URL, the combined proposal for this round should be withdrawn. The exact tablet breakpoint value has not been decided.
versions.change_summary: Record the initial trade-offs for the two changes

# Ridgeway Server Interpolation Proposal

On review, the earlier view that "keeping the template text is safer" is not on firm enough ground. It conflates two questions: whether server variables still need to be visible, and whether the default server's URL should be directly readable. The former concerns editing and understanding; the latter concerns the displayed result. The presence of variables alone is not a reason to rule out substituting default values.

This round of verification still starts at `packages/elements-core/src/hooks/useChosenServerUrl.ts`. That location is a suitable starting point for checking server selection and URL handling, but it is not a substitute for confirming the reference relationships. The initial draft described it as the sole location for the default server; that statement is retained as an earlier judgment and is no longer a basis for deciding where the implementation belongs.

There are currently two candidate approaches.

- Keep the template: continue showing variable placeholders in URL so users can recognize the server template; users will need to look elsewhere for the default values.
- Show default values: when the default server is selected, replace the variables with their corresponding default values before displaying the full URL; variable metadata should still be visible in the editing context.

The second approach is closer to the readability problem this review aims to solve, but it has not yet been specified as the final rule. First confirm that substitution happens at the URL display stage and does not write back to the server template or editor state. If the two are mixed, it may not be possible to distinguish the original template from the displayed address after switching servers.

The tablet responsive breakpoint is also split out from the main proposal. Verify whether the layout at tablet widths can still preserve the selection and the URL area, rather than testing a specific pixel value. The old draft treated the breakpoint as part of the interpolation proposal, but there is no basis for that link; subsequent checks should be separate.

Hold off on submitting changes that implement both items together. If displaying default values requires changing variable metadata, or the tablet layout requires changing server selection, return to separate reviews.
versions.change_summary: Separate the interpolation and breakpoint reviews after reassessment

# Ridgeway Server Interpolation Proposal

This page preserves how the proposal evolved during the Ridgeway 3.4 review. It is not a guide to the page's later behavior. The earliest proposal confused "keeping template variables visible" with "not substituting default values in the displayed address," and tacked the tablet breakpoint onto the same change. That made it easy to discuss both at once, but did not explain what each would affect.

## Conservative approach from the first draft

The old draft proposed keeping the server variable template text in the URL area. The rationale was that variable locations should not disappear from the UI, especially when users still need to determine whether a given server has an editable default value. That rationale only addressed variable visibility; it did not answer whether readers should see the template or a directly usable address once the default server is selected.

The first draft also proposed checking the tablet responsive breakpoint as a side task in the same round of changes. That arrangement was later rejected: the breakpoint handles layout at tablet widths and should not be responsible for server template substitution semantics. Even if both issues occur on the same page, responsive layout must not determine the content of URL.

## Assumptions revised during review

The review narrowed the starting point for investigation to `packages/elements-core/src/hooks/useChosenServerUrl.ts`. It is retained here as an old troubleshooting entry point: it focuses attention on where the selected server and URL meet, rather than on a general search for all server configurations. The first draft's description of this path as the sole implementation location is no longer used. During review, the display location needs to be confirmed by following actual references, rather than inferring the scope of changes from filenames alone.

The comparison at the time was not about "whether variables should exist," but about two display sequences. Keeping the template leaves variable locations visible, but readers have to substitute values themselves to get the result for the default server. Substituting default values first makes the address more complete, but must avoid writing the displayed result back into the template, edit state, or other servers' values. That risk limited interpolation to a candidate display-layer action; it could not simply be extended into rules for editing variables.

The tablet portion was also split out. The check is not for a particular fixed threshold, but whether the selected server, the URL area, and the relevant variable information can still all be identified after the responsive layout contracts. The old proposal did not specify a breakpoint value or give a reason to tie that value to interpolation order. Both gaps remain open so that the discussion at the time is not mistaken for an agreed layout specification.

## Correction retained on this page

The latest on-site feedback overturned the working assumption that "the default server always retains the template." The current requirement is: An explicit interpolation mode replaces each server variable with its default value before displaying the URL.

This requirement is limited to substitution before display in explicit interpolation mode. It does not mean deleting variable metadata, nor does it mean that all servers automatically become the default server. The old draft's concern about template visibility still holds, but it should be addressed by the UI that contains the variable information, rather than by requiring URL to always retain placeholder text.

The candidate changes for Ridgeway 3.4 should therefore continue to be split into two tracks: one deals only with the display timing of default server interpolation; the other only checks layout at the tablet responsive breakpoint. If the former shows signs of writing back to the template or changing server selection, withdraw the display-layer proposal and reconfirm the boundaries. If maintaining the tablet layout requires hiding URL or variable information, interpolation rules must not be used as a workaround either.

Still unconfirmed are the priorities of the different areas after the tablet layout contracts, and what form the variable information should take when the default values are already displayed. These points have not been filled in as a release specification here. They remain open so that subsequent investigation does not start again from the old premise that "both changes must be made together."

# Ridgeway Path Compatibility Migration Procedure

This record is initially for checking path-related Ridgeway 3.4. The existing entry point is at `packages/elements/src/utils/oas/__tests__/oas.spec.ts`, and the test file imports `transformOasToServiceNode` from `../`. At the time, it wasn't treated as a callback-only entry point; it was more like a centralized checkpoint before passing the OpenAPI structure into service node.

The earliest approach was to first check whether the path could reach the operation, then whether the callback received the same path fragment. This order later caused a misreading: ordinary operation paths and callback paths both look like "addresses" on the page, but the former must preserve the literal form written in the spec, while the latter needs to be processed into a usable callback path before display or connection. The two cannot be judged together just because their names are similar.

The migration convention left at the time was brief:

1. Start from the existing OAS test entry point; do not create another path check with the same name.
2. Choose a literal OpenAPI path with punctuation and trace it through the post-transform operation node; do not first change the path into a form you consider neater.
3. Record the callback path separately. If it requires normalization, handle that in its own step; do not substitute the result of the ordinary operation path.
4. When the operation does not appear, first record the input path, operation, and method; do not write only "callback was lost."

An old note says, "As long as the path matches the operation after transform, that's enough." This sentence is retained because it explains why the early tests only cared about traversal; it does not cover literal paths or specify how callback paths are handled.

```
Old check
literal path ──> find operation ──> stop

Proposed migration check
literal path ──> traversal ──> operation node
callback path ──> normalization ──> callback entry
```

Here, "stop" is not a release decision; it only marks where the old check ended in that segment. The follow-up review needs to document the content carried along in node, and where the callback path is normalized.

Open question: If the same input contains both a literal path and a callback, which side's observation should the test establish first? This is not decided in this record.

# Ridgeway Path Compatibility Migration Workflow

`packages/elements/src/utils/oas/__tests__/oas.spec.ts` is still the starting point for this round of review. The direct import in the file has not changed:

```ts
import { transformOasToServiceNode } from '../';
```

This makes the earlier habit of "only checking whether an operation appears" insufficient. The test entry point also covers the local behavior of the OAS transform, while Ridgeway 3.4 requires separate checks of literal OpenAPI path traversal and callback path normalization. They can be covered in the same manual review, but they do not share passing criteria.

## The Retained 2023 Rule

The initial records treated the path as a key for looking up an operation. Operators would start from a OpenAPI path and check whether the corresponding operation node existed after the transform; if it did, they considered that path fully migrated. That was a useful but incomplete working rule. It was good for identifying cases where traversal could not reach the operation at all, but it did not require preserving the original path or checking the request or response information around the operation.

The original wording has not been deleted:

> After a path goes through the transform, it only needs to match an operation.

This statement can no longer serve as a gate for Ridgeway 3.4. This is not because a callback is more complex than a regular path, but because "finding a match" does not show that the literal punctuation in the input is still in the right place. Even an operation that looks normal may have lost the original path needed to trace it back. The old rule is useful only as the first step: confirming that traversal did not stop before reaching the operation.

## The Fork in the Review

This review does not infer the input from the page title or callback wording. First, in the OAS input, pin down one literal OpenAPI path, then follow the results of `transformOasToServiceNode` to inspect operation node. Put the observations in the same record:

- Whether the input path contains punctuation that needs to be recognized exactly as written;
- Whether traversal reaches the operation;
- Whether the operation identifier and method remain recognizable;
- Whether the adjacent request, query, and response content is retained along with the operation;
- Whether the callback path goes through normalization separately, rather than being treated as an alias for a regular path.

There is no requirement here to turn every input into a test matrix. In practice, it is enough to keep one example illustrating a literal path and one callback example. Record their observations separately in the change request; otherwise, investigators may attribute a callback display issue to operation traversal, or conversely treat a path parsing issue as a callback formatting issue.

```
literal OpenAPI path in the input
        │
        ├── transformOasToServiceNode
        │       │
        │       └── operation node
        │              ├── Where to look up the original path
        │              ├── operation / method
        │              ├── request and query
        │              └── response collections
        │
        └── callback path
                └── Proceed to callback-side checks after normalization
```

The diagram above shows the relationships between checks, not that the callback is inserted into operation node. Previously, someone included the callback in the operation validation conclusion because the two branches in the diagram shared an input; that interpretation no longer applies.

## An Issue Left Open

During the review, the initial suspicion was that the literal punctuation issue came from callback path adjustments. After the records for the two sides were separated, that explanation no longer held up: callback path normalization still needs to be checked, but it cannot replace the traversal check on the literal OpenAPI path. The earlier suspicion is retained here because it explains why only a general "path is OK" result was initially recorded.

What could actually be confirmed at the time was that the test file provided an entry point for the transform and could be used to record observations of the path and operation. What had not been confirmed was the exact adjacent step where callback path normalization was completed. That gap cannot be filled by a successful result for a regular path.

## Migration Order

When migrating the old records to the checks for Ridgeway 3.4, add the missing material in the following order:

1. Open the OAS test entry point and confirm that the check uses `transformOasToServiceNode`, not another concept with the same name on the page.
2. Select a literal OpenAPI path and record its literal form in the input; do not manually change the punctuation before recording it.
3. Inspect where traversal lands, and write down the actual observations of operation, method, request, query, and response next to operation node.
4. Take a separate callback path and record its form before and after normalization; do not put this under the results for a regular operation.
5. If the operation does not produce node, return to the input path and method; if the callback is unusable, return to callback path normalization. Treat the two cases as separate stopping points.

The purpose of this order is not to expand the test scope, but to separate two types of failure that were mixed together in the old records. The migrated records should let later readers tell whether a given issue was that traversal did not reach the operation, or that the callback path did not yield a usable result at its own processing step.

## Review Side Notes

During the review, someone asked that "path found" not be written as "path preserved". This feedback has been accepted. The two statements refer to different observations: the former checks whether traversal continues, while the latter checks whether the original path can still be looked up. The earlier draft treated them as the same conclusion, and this has now been corrected.

Another item to retain is the information around the operation. Even when only migrating paths, indicate next to the result whether request, query, and response are still adjacent to the operation; this is not a request to explain their respective structures here, but a way to avoid ending the review based solely on the operation name.

## Retained Legacy Procedure

The following passage is from the old manual and is being kept for now:

> First check whether the callback appears; if it does, the regular path can be considered to have passed.

This passage was overturned by subsequent review. The appearance of a callback does not prove that the exact content of the literal OpenAPI path can still be looked up after traversal, nor does it prove that the information around the operation is complete. It is retained only to explain why old tickets ended up with the contradictory status "callback is OK, path still needs checking".

## One Item Still to Add

Callback path normalization has been included in this page's scope, but the current records do not confirm which layer adjacent to the transform completes it. When adding evidence next time, fill in only this gap, and do not use it as an opportunity to rewrite all of the OAS path handling.

# Ridgeway Path Compatibility Migration Workflow

This page has always been treated as a folder of path-related material for Ridgeway 3.4, rather than a complete OAS manual. The entry point has not moved:`packages/elements/src/utils/oas/__tests__/oas.spec.ts`. Several later rounds of verification all started here, because the file directly imports:

```ts
import { transformOasToServiceNode } from '../';
```

Old links still bring people here, so the early wording and steps have not been cleaned up. They explain why some reports described literal OpenAPI path traversal and callback path normalization as the same issue.

## 2023-06-26: The Original Path Criteria

The initial verification only checked whether the path made it past transform. If the input contained a path, reviewers looked for the corresponding operation; if they found it, they wrote "the path is fine". At the time this could rule out the most obvious failure: the path not entering operation processing at all.

The rule left by that version is reproduced below, unchanged:

> After a path goes through transform, it only needs to match an operation.

This was not entirely wrong in older versions. If no operation was created at all, this statement was enough to prompt a review of path and method first. However, it did not ask whether the punctuation in the input was still recognizable, nor what was left around the operation. When it was later applied to Ridgeway 3.4, it led to the overreaching conclusion that "an operation was found, so the path must be fine".

The old records also treated callback as a shortcut for validating a regular path: as long as there was a result on the callback side, the operation from the same input would also be marked as passed. This practice came from the manual inspection habits at the time, not from a relationship in the implementation. The fact that both types of path appear in the same OAS does not mean they have gone through the same processing.

The sketch from that time is also preserved:

```
path
 │
 ├─ Find operation
 │    └─ Found: done
 │
 └─ callback appears: also counts as done
```

This diagram is no longer suitable for use as an operating procedure. It leaves no room for literal punctuation, and also incorrectly presents the appearance of callback as supporting evidence for a regular operation. It was not deleted, because the source of misjudgments in several subsequent rounds of regression testing could be traced back to this simplified diagram.

## Additional Notes on the On-Call Side Page

A later on-call addendum split "matching" into two questions: whether traversal reaches the operation, and whether the original path can still be looked up. The two questions look similar, but they lead the investigation in different directions.

If traversal does not reach the operation, first check the combination of the input path, operation, and method. If the operation already exists, but the path no longer retains its original literal form in subsequent observations, the case cannot be closed as "found". The first type of issue makes the operation disappear; the second makes the operation appear to exist, but makes lookups and comparisons unreliable.

That addendum did not specify where the callback belonged, and only said: "Record the callback path separately, and do not apply the same conclusions to it and to the ordinary path." This sentence was later retained as the dividing line on this page. It does not claim which function completes callback path processing, but only requires that records made at the time not collapse the two tracks into a single result.

The old checklist still had three very rough checkboxes:

- the path reached the operation;
- the callback appeared to exist;
- the page showed no obvious anomalies.

The third item was later crossed out. Whether the page shows anomalies cannot replace observations on the transform side, nor can it indicate that the callback path has completed normalization. The first two items are no longer sufficient either, but they still remind reviewers to start with the input and operation rather than focusing on the presentation layer first.

## A Misattribution

In one review along the way, the initial suspicion was: the problem with the literal path was caused by callback path cleanup. There were reasons for this guess at the time—both sides were recorded as "path", and the callback's path looked more like something that needed formatting.

Once the records were separated, this assessment was overturned. The traversal of an ordinary operation path and the normalization of a callback path can appear side by side in a single manual review, but the results on one side cannot make up for the other. A callback being usable does not mean that the literal OpenAPI path has been preserved on the operation side; an operation having been created does not mean that the callback path has undergone correct normalization either.

This failure did not yield a generalizable root cause, nor should it be expanded into a complete callback design. It left only one operational change: records must separately state observations of the ordinary path and observations of the callback path. If the only statement is "path is normal", later readers cannot determine which track it actually covers.

The failure notes from that time are still attached here:

```text
Suspicion: callback path cleanup swallowed literal punctuation
Result: observations on the callback side cannot be used to infer conclusions about operation traversal
Change: record the two sides separately, and return to their respective entry points
```

"Result" does not mean that the callback path has no normalization; on the contrary, callback path normalization is still something that needs follow-up on this page. What was abandoned was the approach of using it to explain all literal path anomalies.

## 2024-03-01: Migration Draft

The migration draft splits the old check into two parts. The first part handles literal OpenAPI path traversal: retain the path in the input, do not replace punctuation first, then follow `transformOasToServiceNode` to observe operation node. The second part handles callback path normalization: write the callback path's own input and processing results in a separate record.

The draft listed the following sequence at the time:

1. Use a fixed literal OpenAPI path containing recognizable punctuation.
2. Run the transform or review its results via the OAS test entry point.
3. Confirm that traversal reaches the operation, rather than merely observing that the upstream path is read.
4. Put the observations of the operation and method together with the input path in the same example.
5. Check normalization on the callback path separately, without substituting passing results from a regular path.

The fourth step was expanded later. Early drafts only said "find the operation", without putting the operation's identifier and the method back into the same observation; this would mask one type of failure: the operation node appears to exist, but it cannot be matched to the operation in the original input.

The draft also once said "Normalize path first, then validate transform". This passage is now obsolete. For a literal OpenAPI path, this would prematurely erase the input differences that most need to be preserved. This line is still retained to remind maintainers not to convert samples into a more readable form before review.

```text
Obsolete sequence
Input path ──> Manual normalization ──> transform ──> operation

Preservation order
literal path in the input ──> transform ──> operation node ──> compare again
```

The diagram above only shows the order of the checks; it does not indicate that callback path handling and operation node share any internal storage structures.

## Corrections after the review excerpt

One review pointed out: "path preservation" must not be described as "the path appears unchanged". This feedback changed the wording on this page. Preservation here means that the input path can serve as a back-reference for operation node, not that some text on a page happens to look identical.

The review also pointed out that request, query, and response must not be glossed over in a side note about callback. They are parts surrounding operation that need to be checked together. They have not been split into separate migration targets here, because this page is not a description of each of them; when checking literal OpenAPI path traversal, we only confirm that they remain associated with operation.

This round also corrected an inaccurate conclusion. The old draft said "callback appears first, so the regular path does not need to be checked any further". This was later explicitly marked as no longer applicable. The appearance of callback at most indicates a visible result on the callback side, and cannot replace the traversal record for the literal path.

The side note left after the review reads:

> Write "found" and "preserved" separately. Do not let callback results serve as evidence for the regular path.

This is not an additional procedure, but a point of confusion that must be avoided when recording observations. If there is not enough material to assess one side, leave that side unconfirmed; do not substitute success on the other side.

## Organize old samples before the current checks

When migrating from old records into Ridgeway 3.4, do not start by uniformly rewriting historical samples. If an old sample only says "path is normal", keep it in its original location and add a note alongside it clarifying just what it confirmed. Changing it directly to "literal path has been preserved" would project later understanding back onto the old conclusion.

When organizing them, classify each old observation into one of two categories:

- **Regular operation path**: whether traversal reached the input path, whether an operation was formed, and whether the literal content in the input can be cross-checked against node.
- **callback path**: whether it entered its own normalization check, and whether the record misapplied a conclusion about a regular operation.

Some legacy samples cannot be classified. For example, a sample may only say "callback is working normally" without recording a path or describing the operation. Such samples cannot be used as migration evidence for Ridgeway 3.4, but they do not need to be erased from the history page either. Simply leave them in the legacy section and mark them as not reconstructable.

To prevent reviewers from inferring the input from the wording on the page, sample records should first describe observations of the input, then observations of node after the transform. Put callback entries in a separate paragraph. This way, in a regression involving both, readers can still tell which conclusion belongs to which path.

## Actionable migration steps

### Start with the existing test entry point

Open `packages/elements/src/utils/oas/__tests__/oas.spec.ts` and confirm that the path check being examined this time goes through `transformOasToServiceNode`. Do not jump to the callback page or other path tools just because the name contains OAS; the first paragraph of observations on this page must focus on the results of this transform.

If the entry point does not provide enough samples, record that samples are missing, and do not first use callback results to fill in a judgment about the operation. The test file is the starting point, and you are not required to infer all callers here.

### Preserve the input form of the literal OpenAPI path

When selecting a literal OpenAPI path from the existing samples, first record all punctuation that appears in the input in your observations. Here, "literal" refers to the path form originally written in the specification; it does not mean that reviewers should rewrite the path to make it look nicer.

Do not first remove punctuation, replace separators, or transcribe it into the path string you are used to. Doing so would make the later traversal lose its value as a comparison with the original input, even if it succeeds.

### Check traversal first, then node

During the check, first ask whether traversal reached the operation. If it did not, record the input path, operation, and method, and stop here. Do not enter the callback branch, and do not infer what the operation was supposed to be from the response or the page display.

If traversal has reached the operation, then examine the content left in node. The check here is not "whether there is an operation block on the page", but whether that node can be linked to the original path, operation, and method.

### Cross-check the content around the operation as well

operation node must not be reduced to a name alone. Reviewing the literal path requires also checking whether the request, query, and response collections still follow that operation. They do not need to be expanded into separate new specifications on this page; they are recorded to avoid overlooking cases where adjacent information has already become detached from node merely because the operation exists.

If an observation can only confirm the operation and method, record exactly that here. Do not write request, query, or response as present by default when they were not seen. Conversely, if response collections exist, do not infer from this that the original path must have remained unchanged.

### Separate normalization for callback path

Put the callback path in a separate inspection section. Record the path before it enters normalization and the observations after processing; do not fold it into the results for ordinary operations. If a problem appears on the callback side, first return to normalization of the callback path; if traversal of the ordinary path has a problem, first return to the inspection entry containing `transformOasToServiceNode`.

This step does not require the callback to produce the same node as the ordinary operation, nor does it make the callback result an acceptance criterion for the ordinary path. It merely separates the two inspection tracks that were mixed together in the old record.

### Leave short results that can be rechecked

Each check only needs to leave a few easily identifiable items: the input path, operation, method, the operation node and the surrounding request/query/response observations, and whether the callback path has undergone separate normalization. There is no need to add lengthy background for every example.

A readable result might look like this:

```text
ordinary path: retain the input's literal form; traversal reaches operation;
           operation and method can be rechecked; request/query/response observed along with node.

callback: record path normalization separately; do not use the ordinary path's result as a basis for acceptance.
```

This is not a fixed output format. It only requires that the two types of objects not be crammed into a single "path is normal" statement.
## Card addendum covering the months from 2025-09 to 10

ATC-204 is a task card for the maintenance entry point of the literal OpenAPI path. It requires running literal OpenAPI path traversal through the existing test entry point, and retaining the affected units together with adjacent unchanged units. The card subsequently entered review, with the recorded reason being that the implementation had been completed on an existing branch and sent directly to review. This status does not replace path observation; the literal path, operation landing point and content traceable in node must still be retained.

ATC-220 instead records the callback path maintenance entry point. It began with a rollback check, after which work started again. For this page, the action to carry forward is narrowly scoped: callback path observation must be recorded independently, and the result of the ordinary operation path cannot be used as a substitute. The card requires restoring the missing steps on the callback path normalization page by following one real user flow; it does not present the ordinary operation's pass as proof of callback recovery.

These two cards respectively fill in the two sides that the old records had conflated into the single statement "path is normal". They do not specify ownership for the concrete implementation of callback normalization, so this page continues to record only the inspection boundary and does not turn unseen internal steps into a conclusion.

## Current requirements

After these several rounds of corrections, the requirement in Ridgeway 3.4 for the ordinary operation path is stated as follows: The transformOasToServiceNode OAS traversal keeps literal punctuation in a path and carries the original path, operation id, method, request query, and response collections into the operation node.

This sentence applies only to `transformOasToServiceNode`'s OAS traversal. It does not make the same node structural guarantee for the callback path. The callback path is still recorded according to its own normalization process; checking the two side by side does not mean collapsing them into a single object.

When applying this requirement, the observation order remains input first, then traversal, then operation node. The original path is used for comparison with the input, not a value inferred afterward from the displayed text. The operation id and method need to be associated with the same path; request query and response collections are treated as adjacent content within node that should be retained together.

"literal punctuation" is an aspect of this migration that old habits can easily cause people to overlook. The old approach only checked that a path could reach an operation, often making the input more uniform first when punctuation was encountered. This can no longer be done. The path's literal punctuation should be preserved all the way from the input to the operation node record that can be looked up later.

## An Adjacent Issue Retained Here

callback absence rendering is outside the migration scope of this page. Both it and callback path appear in the materials, so early records occasionally conflated the two. Only callback path normalization is addressed here; how to render absence is covered in a separate resource, which can be found at DOC-16.

This issue has not been split into additional sections for now. It is retained to prevent maintainers from seeing the word callback, adding rendering logic to this page, and thereby once again obscuring observations of path normalization itself.

## Stopping Points During Review

When operation node cannot be found, stop at the records for literal path, operation, and method for now, and do not fill in gaps with callback results. When operation node exists but the original path cannot be looked up, stop at the path preservation issue, and do not write "path passed". When there are not enough observations of callback path normalization, separately mark the callback side as unconfirmed, and do not carry over results from ordinary paths. When request, query, or response collections have not been observed, record only what has been seen.

## Old Paragraph: A Shortcut That No Longer Applies

The shortcut below was once used for checks under time pressure and is now deprecated, but is retained for people reading old tickets:

1. Open callback;
2. If callback has content, mark the path as usable;
3. If there is operation text on the page, stop.

The problem with it is not that callback should not be checked, but that it conflates the visible content of callback, the operation text on the page, and the literal path after transform into a single result. The replacement method now is: check regular paths through `transformOasToServiceNode`'s traversal and operation node, and check callback paths through normalization.

The old shortcut also did not save request query or response collections. When only old conclusions of this kind remain, they should not be dressed up as meeting the current requirements; they can be treated as a trace of someone having looked at callback, but not as a complete record of the literal path.

## Appendix: Excerpts from Old Examples

### Example One: Only Writing "operation found"

Early samples condensed the results for the input path and operation into the single statement "operation found". This kind of record can still help confirm that traversal reached some point at the time, but it cannot show whether punctuation in the path was preserved, nor whether request, query, and response were within the same node. Label: Outdated, cannot be reused directly.

### Example Two: Using callback Instead of Checking the path

Another old example says "callback exists, path is normal". This is a historical observation, not a current assessment. It can show that the reviewer looked at callback at the time, but it left no before-and-after results for callback path normalization, nor any comparison of the literal OpenAPI path's operation node. Label: Later overturned, not to be used as a migration result.

### Example Three: Normalizing the Input First

An old draft suggested converting paths to a uniform format before passing them to transform. This example is retained to show why literal paths need to be migrated separately: once they are normalized in advance, even finding the operation later cannot prove that the original literal punctuation was preserved throughout. Label: No longer used.

If more samples are added later, prefer appending them after the corresponding existing examples rather than rewriting the historical paragraphs above. Each sample only needs to state whether it is a regular operation path or a callback path, what was observed in the input, what was observed after transform or normalization, and whether it stops at an unconfirmed point.
