# Server Editing and Branch Migration Workflow

This record initially placed non-enum server editor and encoded branch lookup on the same Ridgeway 3.4 regression track. The entry point has not changed; what has changed is how the tracks are separated after that point: first return to the TryIt tests, then confirm whether the current fixture actually exposes a server, a branch, a page state, or a request URL. The old issue names still lead to the same place, but they are no longer treated as evidence of a shared implementation.

```text
Old issue name
  -> packages/elements-core/src/components/TryIt/TryIt.spec.tsx
  -> Current fixture or operation
  -> An identifiable page state, path segment, or request URL
```

No "post-migration implementation file" is documented here. The new paths in the available material are only observation routes: from an old name to a test file, and then from the test file to a specific fixture. This distinction must be preserved. A file-level entry point is useful for recovering the test context at the time, not for directly associating a particular name with an implementation.

The dependencies visible at the top of the file are as follows:

```ts
import '@testing-library/jest-dom';
import { Provider as MosaicProvider } from '@stoplight/mosaic';
import { HttpParamStyles, IHttpOperation } from '@stoplight/types';
import { cleanup, render, screen, waitFor } from '@testing-library/react';
```

`MosaicProvider` indicates that a component environment is present during rendering; `render`, `screen`, `waitFor`, and `cleanup` are test-side observation tools. `HttpParamStyles` and `IHttpOperation` bring operation and parameter objects into the vicinity of this test. All of these establish only the test context for TryIt. The record does not identify any of these dependencies as the point where encoded branch lookup occurs, nor does it attribute the act of waiting for a page state to any specific regression.

## The Merged Route Left by the Initial Draft

The initial draft's reasoning was straightforward: both issues might surface in the request address, so migrate them along a single track. This made files quick to find, but collapsed editor state, operation node, path segments, and request URL into the same "result". The old route can still serve as a navigation trail:

```text
non-enum server editor
          \
           -> TryIt.spec.tsx -> Result after one render
          /
encoded branch lookup
```

A shared call relationship cannot now be inferred from this diagram. The path only shows that the old investigation once led here; the initial draft did not preserve the complete fixture, assertion text, or failure output, so locating the file and confirming the regression are two different things. If a later review finds only a single URL, that only shows that the fixture includes an observation of URL; it does not complete the migration of the other name as well.

## The server Track: Separate Default Values from Edited Values

The old record contains the statement "the current version covers non-enum server editor". It is retained as the working description used at the time, but it does not clarify the layer of coverage. For this track, the observation sequence is now:

```text
Open TryIt
  -> Check whether variables are substituted into the default server
  -> Enter server editor
  -> Select or edit a non-enumerated value
  -> Inspect the editor state
  -> Then inspect request URL
```

The presence of default server interpolation does not mean that user-edited values are still retained. The editor displaying a value also does not mean that request URL has used it. If the current fixture exposes only one of these layers, the result stops at that layer. Do not infer an editing action from an example of default substitution, or infer that the control has accepted a non-enumerated value from a change in URL.

The old name non-enum is retained here to refer to cases where a server variable can be edited; it is not equivalent to an enumerated-value selector. The material does not preserve the control name, input format, or a complete variable metadata sample. During review, record whether the server template appears, whether server placeholder visibility is present, and whether request URL is subsequently seen. These are three adjacent observation points, not a single field to be merged.

The initial draft's instruction to "find existing test cases first" is still useful, but after finding one, first identify whether it verifies default substitution or a user-edited server value. Only when the latter has been documented should the fixture be treated as a direct entry point for non-enum server editor. If only default substitution is found, retain that local result rather than upgrading the old description into a claim that the editor regression is covered.

The highlighted result on the page must also be recorded separately. It is only the rendered highlighting context; it cannot stand in for editor state, much less for whether the request uses the edited server value. The old draft classified all page displays as results, making it easy to skip the actual differences when investigating that term later.

## The branch Track: First Confirm Where branch Appears

In the early material, encoded branch lookup has only a name, with no actual call, input sample, or user-visible result. A review did not supply these details, so it remains an unresolved migration branch. An arbitrary URL assertion in the TryIt file cannot be used to fill this gap.

First check whether the fixture actually uses branch as an input or path segment. If it does, record the following layers:

```text
branch input
  -> encoded content enters the lookup
  -> literal OpenAPI path traversal
  -> Path display or lookup result
  -> Request URL (if the fixture includes this observation)
```

This sequence specifies where to observe; it does not predetermine the final string. When a path appears on the page, ordinary text matching is not equivalent to encoded branch lookup; when a request URL is present, it also does not justify inferring that branch was looked up as expected. The existing record does not establish whether branch endpoint and server editor are in the same operation node.

The old route was to return from the name to the test file and count any URL assertion as coverage found. This is still useful for locating the file, but not for judging behavior. The new record separates results into lookup results, path displays, and request URL. If the fixture contains no branch, leave that gap explicit rather than following server variable helper API to speculate about where branch is handled.

## How to Record Findings After Migration

Migration here does not mean copying old tests to another branch. There is no new branch name, migration batch, caller list, or new fixture content to document. The only confirmed change is the observation route:

| Location | Previous usage | Current focus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Issue name | Directly merge the two names | Use as an entry point back to the test file |
| `TryIt.spec.tsx` | Treat as the shared home of both issues | Confirm the test environment and current fixture |
| server observation | Check only whether URL changes | Separate default substitution, editor state, and URL |
| branch observation | Count seeing URL as finding it | Confirm branch input, encoded lookup, and path layers |

The table is not a compatibility matrix, nor does it indicate which callers have switched. If operation or request appears in a later fixture, initially record them only as local objects of that fixture. The test file's revision cannot stand in for a migration batch; which fixture to enter from the file still depends on the references and assertions visible at the time.

When the two tracks meet in the same fixture, their records are no longer merged either. First record the server's default value, editing action, or URL; then record whether branch appears as an input, path segment, or lookup result. Merely having both kinds of objects on the page does not constitute a shared assertion. The resulting record is narrower than "TryIt passes", but it makes clear which layer to start from next time.

## Old Recovery Steps

The old draft recommended returning both items to the old fixture when results differed, then comparing the page displays. This step has not been removed because some people still enter through the old issue names; however, it is no longer a way to determine compatibility.

Old step: return to `TryIt.spec.tsx` and rerun the same page observation.

After returning to the file now, first identify the layer where the difference occurs. For non-enum server editor, the difference may be in default server interpolation, server placeholder visibility, or editor state; for encoded branch lookup, it may be in branch input, literal OpenAPI path traversal, or the final request URL. Comparing only the page's appearance makes it easy to treat identical displays at different layers as the same result.

What is being recovered, therefore, is the investigation route, not the implementation, and this is not a release rollback. When the old fixture and current fixture differ, preserve that inconsistency in the record; do not assume they are equivalent just to reuse the old path. There are no code-level or release-level rollback steps here.

## Observations Still Missing

- The actual call for encoded branch lookup has not been excerpted;
- The specific fixture corresponding to non-enum server editor was not saved;
- The page state that `waitFor` actually waits for was not recorded;
- The specific role of `HttpParamStyles` in this regression is unconfirmed;
- Whether branch endpoint shares operation node with server editor is unconfirmed;
- There is no material available for listing the old and new migration batches or external callers.

These gaps do not prevent returning from the old names to the test file. If actual calls are added later, place them under their respective branches and state whether the observation is an editor state, lookup result, path segment, or request URL; do not combine the two items into a single URL regression again.

# Grouped Request Security Row Decision Record

For this Ridgeway 3.4 requirement, start by tracing where security schemes are rendered. The old investigation notes point to `packages/elements-core/src/components/Docs/HttpService/SecuritySchemes.tsx`. This is a suitable starting point for the follow-up: its name matches the security schemes in the request documentation and keeps the discussion focused near a specific component. At this stage, the source of each row on the page cannot be determined from the file path alone, much less can the path be treated as proof that an upstream model already exists.

There were two options at hand. The first was to retain the per-scheme presentation. It stays close to the existing security scheme objects, and the name shown to readers is easy to associate with an individual scheme. The trade-off is that when a request has a group of related security requirements, the page has no identifiable object that explains the relationship between them.

The second option was to put the security requirements associated with the same request into one row, provisionally called grouped request security row. This is closer to the requirement description, but "put into one row" does not itself define the row's identity. First distinguish the request's operation, the security group represented by the row, the schemes appearing in the row, and any credential hint that may be displayed; they are not the same thing. If one scheme name is used directly to represent the entire row, the scheme name may be mistaken for the group name.

The tentative choice is to use the second option as the subject of further discussion: the requirement record retains grouped request security row instead of reverting to an issue about discussing only individual schemes. This choice does not mean the page already displays items by group, nor does it mean the old one-row-per-scheme display is invalid. The individual scheme remains an object that must be understood during the follow-up; only after confirming what happens before and after the data enters the component can the relationship between the new and old rows be determined.

If handling of individual security schemes can be seen near the file, the next question is where grouping occurs, not to change the row title first. If grouping comes from further upstream, this component may only render it; if grouping is formed inside the component, ordering, names, and empty values need to be reviewed as well. Without these materials, the visual arrangement cannot be written up as though the security semantics have already been merged.

Do not yet specify the field source for group identity, and do not yet assume that the credential placeholder is the group's identity. Review the references and component adjacency for that revision to confirm where the name on the row comes from, whether the multiple schemes really belong to the same group, and whether the old single-scheme entry can still be located. During a later review, the discussion was split into separate layers. The first was the requirement object: what Ridgeway 3.4 wanted to retain was the grouped request security row. The second was row identity: what exactly identifies this row on the page. Only the third was the implementation entry point: whether `SecuritySchemes.tsx` receives data that has already been grouped, or handles individual schemes locally. If these three layers are collapsed into the single phrase "display security schemes in groups," it becomes easy for the requirement name, data source, and rendered result to stand in for one another.

## The Choice Initially Preserved

Neither of the two directions in the initial draft was described as clearly wrong. Keeping individual scheme rows had practical value: each row closely matched the name and data shape of a specific security scheme, allowing readers to trace the row's contents back to an individual object. For the old page, this display also did not require introducing a new group name first. The problem was that, if the security requirements associated with a request needed to be understood as a group in the first place, listing schemes row by row would not tell readers which objects formed the same request-level relationship.

The value of introducing a grouped request security row was not simply to reduce the number of rows. It gave the "relationship between a request and a set of security requirements" its own place on the page. Such a row could have a group identity, retain the related schemes within the same row, and provide a place for subsequent credential hints to belong. But these were possibilities that needed to be validated separately, not facts that followed automatically from the requirement object's name. The appearance of a row in an interface does not mean that the row already has a stable source of identity.

The approach that was not accepted at the time was to treat "multiple schemes in the same row" directly as the completion criterion. That would treat visual compression as semantic grouping. If a row merely places several old objects side by side, without a distinguishable security group identity, readers still cannot tell why that row represents those objects. Conversely, if a group identity does exist, using the first scheme's name as the group name may obscure the distinction between the group and the scheme.

Therefore, the decision on this page remains narrowly scoped: continue treating the grouped request security row as the subject of the requirements for Ridgeway 3.4; do not reduce it to "a new layout for several schemes"; and do not declare the group model settled without a source for its fields. This decision preserves the subject of the discussion, but does not supply the missing relationships needed for implementation.

## Review Locations and Visible Adjacencies

The path currently available for review is:

`internal/atlas-console@v_prev/packages/elements-core/src/components/Docs/HttpService/SecuritySchemes.tsx`

The direct dependencies visible in the file header are as follows:

```ts
import { Box, NodeAnnotation, Panel, PanelProps } from '@stoplight/mosaic';
import { HttpSecurityScheme } from '@stoplight/types';
import { sortBy } from 'lodash';
import React from 'react';
```

These imports provide local clues. `Box`, `NodeAnnotation`, `Panel`, and `PanelProps` indicate that this file uses Mosaic's layout, annotation, or panel capabilities at the component level. `React` indicates that it is a React component file. `HttpSecurityScheme` indicates that nearby security scheme data is represented by this type. `sortBy` indicates that sorting is an operation to watch for in the vicinity of this file. Together, they support tracing back from this component, but are not enough to establish where request-level grouping has already been completed.

In particular, `HttpSecurityScheme` must not be equated with a security group. Its name points to a single HTTP security scheme; the current material provides neither a confirmed group model nor a field that places multiple `HttpSecurityScheme` in the same row. The type import can help locate scheme-related processing, but cannot replace an answer to "what this row represents".

`sortBy` also needs to be interpreted cautiously. It only shows that a sorting dependency is visible, not whether sorting happens before or after grouping. If groups are formed first and then sorted, we need to distinguish whether the groups or the schemes within them are being sorted; if sorting is always applied to individual schemes, group identity cannot be inferred from the sorting results alone. The presence of sorting is useful for verification, but does not justify writing that aggregation behavior is already established.

Mosaic panel dependencies likewise do not mean that a group container already exists. A `Panel` can hold a single scheme, or it might hold a request-level entry; the file header cannot resolve this distinction. The presence of `NodeAnnotation` only shows that the component has annotation-related UI nearby, and does not justify asserting that it provides identity cues. Recording these local declarations is intended to reduce misinterpretation during review, not to infer page functionality from the import list.

Older investigation notes point to this file through the issue and call names, so it remains the most appropriate starting point for a search. If subsequent references show that group relationships are formed further upstream, this page does not need to treat its earlier description of the entry point as incorrect; the file was never documented as the sole owner. What needs correcting is the kind of conclusion that misrepresents "finding the file" as "finding the source of the grouping."

## Names, identities, and hints are not the same thing

At least four terms in this requirement are likely to appear close together in discussions: operation, security group identity, scheme identity, and credential placeholder. They should be kept separate. operation indicates which request the current page fragment belongs to; security group identity points to the row represented by a set of security requirements; scheme identity points to a security scheme displayed within a group or on its own; credential placeholder is the placeholder content used for credential input or suggestions. They may appear together in the final UI, but they are not sources for one another.

group identity is the part most likely to be oversimplified away in this work. If a row heading uses only the name of a scheme, readers still see the identity of an individual scheme. It is only appropriate to call it the group's identity when the name or another visible identifier actually comes from a set of security requirements. The material does not provide a specific field name, so this record does not assign it one or label arbitrary display text as group identity.

security group identity is intended to make a grouped row distinguishable, not to turn multiple schemes into a single scheme. If a row contains more than one scheme, the group identity should help readers understand why those schemes appear in the same request entry; it does not have to replace the names of the schemes within the group. This distinction means that subsequent reviews cannot look only at the heading: they must also check whether the heading obscures the original identities of the objects within the row.

credential placeholder also cannot be used to disprove the existence of a group. If a credential hint is empty, it may simply mean that the hint information was not generated; this does not imply that the request has no security group. Conversely, the presence of a placeholder on the page does not automatically mean that it is the only source of credentials for this set of security requirements. Hints, row identities, and scheme lists need to be verified by tracing their respective data adjacencies.

With the terminology separated this way, the choice made in May becomes easier to interpret: the decision was not "a particular name should appear in a particular component," but "request-level grouping should be retained as a distinct requirement object." Where the names come from, whether there are multiple names, and who the hints belong to remain local questions that the review must answer.

## Post-review addendum

The history for ATC-211 includes a `interface_reviewed` action on 2025-10-03. On the same day, the work status moved from To Do to In Progress. The former shows that this interface had come to reviewers' attention, while the latter shows that work had begun. The two actions occurred in sequence, but neither is evidence that the grouped row had been implemented or that the fields had been finalized.

This distinction was added later. The early draft described "add one follow-up check" only as a single overall TODO, making it easy to read review and the start of work as the same kind of progress. Looking back at what actually happened, a review can expose object-naming issues, and starting work can mean beginning changes or an investigation; both can still leave the same behavioral gap. Presenting a status change as a release conclusion would be more misleading than leaving it out.

The public comment dated 10/6 contained only one narrowly scoped statement: one aspect of the grouped request security row was still unconfirmed. The comment did not specify whether that aspect was the row name, grouping conditions, order within a group, credential hints, or the mapping between the component and the requirement object. This page retains that unknown, but does not invent a precise answer on the comment's behalf.

What this comment changed was the approach to closure, not the requirement object. Before it, an actual follow-up check could be treated as the next step; after it, the status of "one aspect still unconfirmed" should be retained until concrete material explains what it is. In Progress cannot close this gap, and neither can an interface review. Card ATC-211 is used to look back at these historical actions, not to replace component-level verification.

When you need to refer to the interface discussion about security group identity, go to DOC-23. The existence of DOC-23 does not change this page's scope: this page preserves the trade-offs for the grouped request security row and the paths for follow-up verification, without reopening the design discussion in another document. Conversely, if actual field sources are later added to this page, that section should not be inserted into the action log for ATC-211 either.

## A few situations that can skew judgment

The first case to consider separately is a request with only one security scheme. It may still appear as a single scheme row, or it may be placed in a grouped row. If it is placed in a grouped row, whether the additional identity provided by the new row conveys any information depends on the current display logic, not on the word grouped. We cannot assume that single-scheme requests and multi-scheme requests have the same group semantics just to make all requests look consistent.

Another case is a request associated with multiple security requirements, none of which has a name that clearly represents the entire group. If the first scheme name is displayed as the row name, the page can render, but readers may mistakenly think that the entire group is equivalent to the first scheme. This is a typical risk of conflating group identity with scheme identity. Without seeing where the name comes from, we cannot call this display approach correct grouping.

We also need to consider the case where a group exists but the credential prompt is empty. A missing credential placeholder only indicates that there is no visible value at the prompt level yet; it cannot be used to rule out a group relationship. Likewise, even if a prompt is present, it is not enough on its own to conclude that the request has only one scheme. Tying whether the prompt is displayed to whether the group exists would misinterpret null handling at two different levels as a single check.

Sorting is the fourth case that can easily be obscured by visual results. At present, all we know is that `sortBy` is one of this file's direct dependencies. If the display order of multiple schemes is stable, we cannot directly conclude that they were grouped first; if the order changes, we cannot directly conclude that the grouping rules have changed either. We first need to identify what is being sorted, then determine whether the ordering is within groups, between groups, or still driven by the old sorting of individual schemes.

The fifth case involves page context. Security rows that look the same may each belong to a different operation. The current material provides no rules for merging across operation boundaries, so we cannot infer that they belong to the same security group just because they are adjacent on the page or have the same text. Request-level relationships must be supported by actual data adjacency, not by similar appearances in screenshots.

These cases are neither production incident reports nor confirmed test samples. They mark the counterexample boundaries that this decision must respect: do not extrapolate grouping semantics from a single visual observation, do not elevate a local name into the identity of the entire group, and do not interpret an empty prompt as the absence of a security relationship.

## Statements retained but no longer used

"The old investigation notes point to this file, so the problem is in this file" was the first oversimplification to emerge. It is retained as a historical search habit, but is no longer used as a basis for decisions. Similarities among the file name, issue name, and call name are enough to make `SecuritySchemes.tsx` a reasonable starting point; actual ownership still depends on how data enters the component, whether the component transforms that data, and where row identity is formed.

"A grouped request just displays multiple schemes on the same row" is no longer sufficient either. This statement captures a possible result on the page, but does not explain how a row becomes an identifiable request-level object. Without group identity, it may describe only a layout change to the old rows; with group identity, we also need to establish whether it is stable, where it comes from, and whether it could conflict with scheme names.

"Adding a title is enough to meet the requirement" was likewise set aside. A title can at most improve readability, not establish a correspondence between a request and its security requirements. In particular, when a request contains multiple schemes, an overly broad title may hide omitted objects; an overly specific title may instead misrepresent one scheme as the entire group. Title wording is not a completion criterion accepted by this page.

"The relevant types have already been imported, so types define the grouping boundary" was not adopted either. `HttpSecurityScheme` allows tracing back to local objects related to security schemes, but does not prove that it is the model for a group. Similarly, the component's use of `Panel` does not prove that Panel is a group container. The import list is a clue for reading the code, not something to extrapolate into a conclusion about data design.

These claims were not deleted because they explain why it later became necessary to explicitly distinguish the object layer, identity layer, and implementation layer. If they were deleted, readers would see only the final cautious conclusions, but would find it harder to understand where the original leaps occurred. Retaining the old claims does not mean allowing them to continue to serve as grounds for closing the issue.

## Compatibility costs

After choosing a grouped request security row, the old single-scheme entry point cannot be ignored. Existing readers may understand the page content through scheme names, or use an individual scheme to locate a request. If the new row retains only the group identity, the visibility of the old names and the way they are used to locate requests may change; if the new row also retains scheme names, it must avoid making scheme names look like group names. The current material does not indicate which backward-compatible presentation has been approved, so this section only records the costs and does not prescribe the final layout.

Sorting is also part of the compatibility cost. If the previous logic processed `HttpSecurityScheme` item by item, introducing request-level rows requires at least determining whether the original sorting still applies to objects within a group. Sorting groups first and then the schemes within them, versus sorting schemes first and then organizing them by request, may produce different page results when names are duplicated or missing. The material does not provide the actual sorting code, so we cannot choose an order for it; but this point must be examined explicitly during review.

Null values and fallback handling pose the same problem. A missing group identity, an empty set of schemes within a group, an inability to generate a name, and an inability to generate a credential hint may require different display paths. Collapsing all of them into "no security information" would lose the objects to trace back to; forcing all of them to be displayed as a group would create an identity that does not exist. This page only requires observing these states separately before confirming the behavior, and does not supply default rules for the implementation.

There is another smaller but practical cost: terminology migration. If older records have consistently described things in terms of individual schemes, a grouped row added later must not cause old entries to be suddenly relabeled as security group. Historical records can still retain the original term scheme; when a new row object appears, explain whether it corresponds to a request, a group, or a scheme. Terminological consistency should not be achieved by retroactively rewriting old facts.

## Current review status

What can currently be confirmed is that both the requirement target and the local verification entry point have been preserved. The requirement target is grouped request security row; the entry point is `packages/elements-core/src/components/Docs/HttpService/SecuritySchemes.tsx`; the locally visible adjacencies include the Mosaic component, `HttpSecurityScheme`, `sortBy`, and React. These facts are sufficient to establish the order for follow-up checks and to avoid broadening the issue back to the entire security page.

What cannot currently be confirmed is the field source for group identity, whether security group identity has already been established before reaching the component, whether the component performs aggregation locally, where sorting occurs relative to grouping, and the exact relationship between the credential placeholder and this row. The review and work-start actions for ATC-211 have not filled these gaps; the comment on 10 6 instead explicitly notes that one point remains unconfirmed.

Representing this page's current assessment through state relationships is more accurate than marking it as "completed":

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  state "Single-scheme observation" as Single
  state "grouped row requirement target" as Grouped
  state "Row identity pending verification" as Pending
  state "Current behavior confirmed" as Confirmed

  [*] --> Single
  Single --> Grouped: Preserve the requirement target
  Grouped --> Pending: Do not infer from file location
  Pending --> Confirmed: Find data adjacencies
  Pending --> Single: Only local types visible
```

Confirmed in the diagram is not the current state, nor is it a release assessment. It only illustrates this: only after finding the actual data adjacencies and the source of row identity can "requirement target preserved" advance to "current behavior confirmed". Returning from Pending to Single means that if verification reveals only local types or single-scheme handling, these still need to be distinguished from the grouping relationship, and verification cannot end prematurely.

## Decisions made on this page

The decision in this version is to continue using grouped request security row as the requirement target name for Ridgeway 3.4. This target name preserves the intent of request-level grouping and no longer reduces the issue to "the display style of a particular scheme". Choosing it does not negate the value of an individual scheme: an individual scheme remains a unit of observation that must be retained when checking back through data, names, and legacy entry points.

This version also decides to retain `SecuritySchemes.tsx` as a starting point for verification, rather than record it as the sole implementation location. The local declarations in that file are enough to show where to start looking; they are not enough to conclusively determine call direction, the source of grouping or the final row structure. If a later review finds that the actual aggregation takes place elsewhere, the decision on this page still stands, and only the actual relationships need to be added.

This version does not merge group identity, security group identity, scheme identity and credential placeholder into a single concept. If later material can confirm the source of one of these, only information about the corresponding object should be added, without taking the opportunity to declare the others known as well. The reason for this is not terminological pedantry, but that these objects affect different compatibility issues: row identity affects how distinguishable groups are, scheme identity affects old names, and hints affect how credential input is presented.

This version also decides not to infer implementation completeness from card status. The interface_reviewed and In Progress statuses of ATC-211 can indicate that discussion, review and action have taken place; they cannot indicate that grouping rules, display names or fallback paths have been implemented. The "one unconfirmed point" on the card remains unchanged, until material is available that can pinpoint the gap.

## What to Look at First When Rechecking

First start with the local declarations and adjacent references in `SecuritySchemes.tsx`, and check whether the data entering the component already carries an identifiable group identity. If the input is still just a single `HttpSecurityScheme`, further investigation is needed to determine whether grouping takes place further upstream, takes place locally, or whether this layer is not yet represented in the current revision. Simply finding multiple scheme objects is no substitute for making this determination.

Second examine what the component does with ordering and names. `sortBy` is a clearly visible adjacency, so identify what is being sorted, rather than merely recording that "sorting exists". If you see a display name, also distinguish whether it refers to a request, a group or an individual scheme. A name can help readers identify a row, but it does not automatically become that row's group identity.

Third look at the relationship between individual schemes and a grouped row. The key point is not how many rows the page ultimately has, but why a row represents these objects. Observe how a request with only one scheme is displayed, whether multiple schemes share a visible name, what is retained when hints are empty, and how readers distinguish duplicate names, and record each of these observations in the actual results.

Only at the fourth step should compatibility with old entry points be addressed. If scheme names can still help locate the same request, record how they appear; if only new group names remain on the page, also record the effect on the old way of reading it. The current material provides no actual commands, environment or execution results, so this page does not invent a verification method. After an actual review takes place, attach the actual revision, environment and failure points from that time, rather than adding a blanket statement that it passed.

## What Remains Open

"One point is still unconfirmed" remains the only explicit description of the gap. It may concern row identity, within-group order, the credential placeholder, or the mapping between the requirement object and the implementation entry point; the material does not provide enough information to narrow it down to any one of these. These four possibilities are listed to prevent them from being substituted for one another during the next check, not to expand the comment into four identified issues.

If the next review only establishes that a grouped row exists on the page, we should still ask what that row represents. If it only establishes that the file uses `HttpSecurityScheme`, we should still ask where the grouping comes from. If it only establishes that sorting exists, we should still ask whether sorting happens before or after grouping. Each partial observation may be valuable, but none can close the gap in this decision record on its own.

The initial May draft will remain in the version history because it accurately records the original choice: first preserve request-level grouping as the requirement object, then return to the specific components to find supporting evidence. The October addendum did not rewrite it as a completion report, but only added the post-review status, counterexamples, compatibility costs, and a clearer stopping point. What can be finalized now is the decision on object naming and entry points for verification; what cannot be finalized now is the specific row identity of the grouped request security row.

# Security Group Identity Proposal

The Ridgeway 3.4 review started with the authentication panel in TryIt. The page had a set of security-related content, but whether a "group" meant a grouping of protocol objects, a presentation-layer grouping, or a name already prepared by the caller had not been distinguished. The early draft therefore focused on the internals of the `Auth.tsx` component, assuming that changing the display there would be enough. That assessment is retained below and must not be treated as a confirmed implementation fact.

> Earlier assessment: security group identity may be determined directly by security data processed inside the component; change the display layer first.

The file review still starts with `packages/elements-core/src/components/TryIt/Auth/Auth.tsx`. The directly visible dependencies are:

```ts
import { Button, Menu, MenuItems, Panel } from '@stoplight/mosaic';
import { HttpSecurityScheme } from '@stoplight/types';
import { flatten } from 'lodash';
import * as React from 'react';
```

These imports show that the Auth component deals with UI, security scheme types, and flattening, but file location alone does not establish ownership of group identity. `flatten` may only prepare rendering data, or it may take part in assembly; the available material is not enough to classify it as a naming rule. The proposal review should first treat "how the data is grouped" and "what name the page displays" as two separate questions.

## Options Under Consideration

**Option A: Continue processing inside the component.** Add stable group identifiers to the security data already available to the Auth component, then pass them to the menu or panel for display. The advantages are a centralized entry point and a small scope for experimentation; existing pages probably would not need to change how they call it right away. The drawback is that the component would handle both data merging and display. If another entry point later reuses the same group, a separate naming scheme may emerge again.

This option can only be treated as a limited experiment. It should not also change request headers, credential placeholders, or the actual contents of security schemes; the display order of those objects and credential suggestions are adjacent issues. In particular, the exception boundaries for suggested request credentials are documented separately in [DOC-24](DOC-24) and must not be settled as part of this page's group identity proposal.

**Option B: Have upstream explicitly provide the identity.** Auth only consumes established group identifiers, with the component responsible for the menu, panel, and selected state. This makes the responsibilities easier to explain, and tests can directly supply groups and names as input. However, it first requires establishing how the component is actually called; if existing callers do not have this field, the change involves more than adding a property to `Auth.tsx`. The call boundary has not yet been verified, so this option cannot be described as a completed migration.

Another compromise was mentioned but not adopted: use the name of the first security scheme as the group name. This appears to avoid a new parameter, but makes array order the source of identity. Multiple schemes, empty names, and schemes with the same name would all make the result unstable, so it is not being adopted as the default option. If it is tried later, these inputs must be listed separately; one normal example cannot stand in for verification.

## Provisional Scope After Review

This page recommends verifying one small point first: at the existing Auth entry point, is the group identifier already present in the incoming data, or is it assembled on the fly inside the component from the flattened results? If the results support the view that the component already has a field for this, option A can be adopted first, with naming logic limited to this entry point; if the field comes from upstream, switch to option B rather than duplicating the rule in the rendering layer. Neither outcome implies that request credential contents need to change.

Verification should leave a record comparing actual inputs and outputs, rather than just checking whether a name appears on the page. At a minimum, it must distinguish a single scheme, multiple schemes, an empty group name, and multiple groups coexisting. The purpose here is not to build a complete compatibility matrix, but to find the first counterexample that breaks "the first item is the group name." Until those counterexamples are available, option A cannot be declared to have solved the identity problem.

If the option A experiment causes different entry points to display different names, remove the new in-component naming logic, restore the original data path to the menu and panel, then switch to the upstream-field option. If option B requires callers to change their interfaces but they cannot provide a stable field in this round, defer the change, keep the old display, and record the gap; do not hide an unknown identity behind a default string.

## Still Open

- The callers of `Auth.tsx` and the structure passed in from upstream have not yet been confirmed on this page.
- Whether security group identity naming should come from the data model or the presentation layer is still undecided.
- There is no example yet showing whether menu items and the selected state share the same identity when multiple groups coexist.
- No decision has been made on handling empty and duplicate names.

This page therefore remains a proposal record, not a statement of the current interface rules. Follow-up review should start with real inputs at the Auth entry point; if the relationships found contradict the earlier assessment, retain the old paragraphs and explicitly revise the assessment alongside the new findings.

# Authentication Placeholder Migration Workflow

This record originally contained just one working assessment: authentication placeholder output already present in legacy calls must not be silently erased during the migration check for Ridgeway 3.4. The first draft did not break down what "preservation" involved, nor did it list which calls were already exercised by tests. That wording was useful as a reminder not to overlook anything, but it was not enough to support a pre-release review.

The original starting point for verification is still in use: `packages/elements-core/src/components/TryIt/TryIt.spec.tsx`. It is not an index of the entire authentication implementation, but a location in nearby test code where this check can be anchored. They are enough to show that this record should focus on rendered output and assertions made while waiting, rather than turning the migration into an explanation of authentication protocols:

```ts
import '@testing-library/jest-dom';
import { Provider as MosaicProvider } from '@stoplight/mosaic';
import { HttpParamStyles, IHttpOperation } from '@stoplight/types';
import { cleanup, render, screen, waitFor } from '@testing-library/react';
```

Among these, `MosaicProvider`, `IHttpOperation`, and the test tools are related items directly visible when opening the file for this review. They can help locate existing fixtures and rendering entry points; seeing an import alone is not evidence that the placeholder has been preserved. What actually needs to be compared is whether the path being migrated still exposes the visible output from the legacy call or example for the current tests to observe.

## Migration Target Left by the Earlier Notes

The early notes described the scope as "auth placeholder preservation". At the time, there was no need to interpret placeholders as default credentials, nor should they have been conflated with header directionality. This check concerns whether the placeholder output originally visible to the caller still exists when authentication information has not yet been provided; it is not about filling in a credential on the caller's behalf, nor about adding a uniform display for all forms of authentication.

Therefore, begin the migration by retaining a legacy call or existing example as a reference. The reference must have a specific input location and visible output; simply writing "authentication works" is not enough. If the earlier notes contain only the issue name, first return to the corresponding example or test fixture to establish that pairing. Without an input-output pair, even passing assertions cannot show that they cover the original placeholder.

```text
Legacy call / Existing example
        │
        │ Preserve the same state with no authentication information provided
        ▼
Visible authentication placeholder output
        │
        │ Review at the current test entry point
        ▼
packages/elements-core/src/components/TryIt/TryIt.spec.tsx
        │
        ├── Observed by existing assertions: record as a traceable migration result
        └── No matching test location: retain as a user path awaiting coverage
```

This diagram shows the checking sequence, not the runtime structure of the components. Its sole purpose is to avoid changing test wording first and then working backward to determine what the legacy call was actually observing. Once placeholder migration is reduced to test names alone, the most likely misjudgment is that the tests still exist, but the output that originally needed to be preserved has been replaced by a different display.

## Moving from Legacy Calls to the Current Test Entry Point

The first step is to find an existing call or example. It must clearly be in a state where authentication information has not been provided, and its output must actually contain a placeholder that needs to be preserved. If the material only shows that the call passes through TryIt, it cannot count as a reference. The migration record should state whether the call comes from an example or a fixture, which output region is being observed, and whether the observation occurs after rendering or after an asynchronous wait. There is no requirement to reconstruct the complete request in every record; the requirement is only that someone later can return to the same local path.

The second step is to open `TryIt.spec.tsx` and look near the existing rendering setup and assertions for a location corresponding to that reference. `render`, `screen`, `waitFor`, and `cleanup` are all direct dependencies of the file, so record synchronously visible output separately from output that appears only after waiting. A placeholder that exists before the wait but disappears afterward is a different migration issue from one that never appears at all; if the existing material does not show which applies, leave it unconfirmed rather than substituting tool names for observation.

The third step is to confirm that the operation data used by the tests has not changed "no authentication information provided" into another state during migration. `IHttpOperation` appears among the test file's dependencies, indicating that operation is a related item worth revisiting; this does not justify inventing fields, headers, or authentication configuration. During the check, trace only what the current fixtures actually express, and preserve the legacy call's precondition through to the assertions.

Only the fourth step is to add assertions or adjust fixtures. The adjustment should target that specific user path, rather than combining all authentication scenarios into one large assertion. An assertion that demonstrates placeholder preservation is more useful than a generic check that the component has rendered. If credentials are added to the input to make an assertion pass, this record should stop there: it is verifying output with credentials, no longer the original placeholder output.

The fifth step is to record the context needed for the release review. Retain at least the version checked, the environment, and the CI job; a local observation missing any one of these can help locate the issue, but cannot serve on its own as the basis for a release decision. There is no need to copy the entire log here. Record the failure point, the corresponding reference call, and the visible output, so that a transient failure is not mistakenly written up as a conclusion about all authentication paths.

## Acceptable Results and Paths Still Needing Coverage

The results of this check can be divided into two categories. In the first, an existing call or example has a corresponding observation in the current nearby test code, and passing was not achieved by supplying new credentials. These results can serve as local samples of migration work that has been reviewed. In the second, the legacy call still indicates placeholder output, but no corresponding location can be found between the existing tests and examples. This is not synonymous with "no problem" and should explicitly remain an uncovered path.

The related card ATC-214 is used to hold the latter category of paths. The card's local description requires triggering the behavior with existing tests or examples and writing back the user paths that are not yet covered; the card should therefore contain the path itself and the missing observation, not just the three words "add missing tests". After this review, the card has been marked release_classified. This classification means it is within the scope of the release check, not that every uncovered path has been completed.

When filling in ATC-214, the following minimum level of detail is recommended:

| Record item | Content to enter |
| --- | --- |
| Reference | Local entry point for the legacy call, example, or fixture |
| Precondition | State with no authentication information provided |
| Observation | Placeholder output that must remain visible |
| Current test location | The nearby test location found in `TryIt.spec.tsx`, or "not found" |
| Gap | A user path that cannot yet be triggered by existing examples |

The table does not replace actual assertions. It breaks a vague "authentication compatibility" claim into traceable local migration items, and lets subsequent reviews distinguish observed output from output that has appeared only in issue descriptions.

## Two Ways to Go Off Track

The first is to start classifying scenarios in bulk by authentication type or field name. This quickly produces a seemingly complete list of scenario names, without revealing what the legacy calls actually exposed. For the subject of this check, matching names do not mean matching placeholder output. An existing example or fixture can serve as a migration reference only if it actually preserves the same precondition.

The second is to treat header-related results as substitute evidence for authentication placeholders. DOC-26 records local verification of operation header directionality. It can provide navigation for adjacent checks, but should not replace the observations here. Correct header directionality does not automatically show that placeholder output is still present when authentication information has not been provided; the reverse is also true. Both pages can be consulted together, but each conclusion still applies to its own subject.

There is also a subtler deviation: marking placeholder migration complete after confirming only that the component can be rendered. The presence of `MosaicProvider` in the file does not mean that all reference outputs have appeared. Provider, operation data, and waiting steps together form the context for reviewing the tests; this record does not elevate any one of them into a universal cause, but only requires that they not be skipped during review.

## Restoring the Legacy Path

If the migrated tests can no longer observe the legacy call's placeholder output, first restore a state that preserves that legacy call or example, then inspect which part of the fixtures, rendering setup, and assertions changed the precondition. The goal of restoration is to recover the original visible output, not to delete failing assertions or change the test input to include credentials.

After restoration, first repeat the check for the same reference call. If the placeholder reappears but there is still no reliable corresponding location in the current tests, do not use the restoration result to close the gap; write the path back to ATC-214 and wait for a test or example that can observe it to be added. If restoration also fails to reproduce the old output, the record should retain the status "legacy call output not reproduced" and include the version checked, the environment, and the CI job, so that results from two different sets of conditions are not later combined into a single conclusion.

The earlier draft did not clearly describe this restoration action, which made "preserving the old output" sound like an abstract requirement. Restoration is now included in the migration steps so that a concrete route for tracing back remains after changes are made: return first to the legacy call, then to the test entry point, and then determine whether the gap lies in the fixtures, observation timing, or a user path that is not yet covered.

## Stopping Point After This Review

This page maintains only the migration check for auth placeholder preservation. The available material supports separating the test entry point, reference, observation, and gap, and also supports writing uncovered paths back to ATC-214; it does not list the specific fixtures and outputs for every user path, so no such list is invented here. Future additions should start from the paths in the card and return to existing examples or `TryIt.spec.tsx`, rather than expanding from a general conclusion about authentication.

The remaining unconfirmed item is which legacy calls can already be triggered directly by existing tests or examples, and which calls are mentioned only in the earlier notes. This does not prevent using the local results already found as references, but it does affect the assessment of coverage before release.

# Quality Signal Dashboard Cache Trade-off Decision Record

This decision originally recorded a very narrow choice: when faced with failure samples from the Quality Signal Dashboard, preserve the existing state, or set up a separate environment and try again. The earlier draft phrased this as "leave the current revision unchanged," which later made it easy to read as "do not rerun" or "the cache is already reliable." Neither reading is correct. What is being preserved is the state on which the assessment rests; whether a rerun can be performed under controlled conditions is a separate matter.

The earlier draft also included discussion of `variable metadata` and `response selector`. This was a proposed direction for splitting things out to examine the failure exit paths at the time, not an implementation change that had already been completed. This paragraph is retained because it explains why not all differences were attributed to a single variable: the two exit paths did not appear to be the same at the time. It cannot, in turn, establish that the callers of `editor state` are already known, nor can it replace checking the actual callers.

## This Decision

Continue to retain the current revision as a reference for the original state, and do not rebuild the environment just to supply a missing command.

This decision applies to this Quality Signal Dashboard record, not to the build environment for the entire project, nor is it a conclusion about all consumers. Rebuilding the environment can produce a new sample, but when the original command parameters are incomplete and the permission conditions remain unsettled, that sample cannot automatically be linked back to the old record. At most, it provides a new comparison; it cannot replace the original state.

Accordingly, controlled reruns are allowed, but they must be recorded separately as comparison material. The constraint recorded in ATCA-015 is to hold elements-core-quality-signal, the current entry point, and the command fixed, replacing only the current revision; the card states, "The comparison changes only one condition." The value of this constraint is not in seeking an impressive result from a single run, but in letting later readers know exactly how the new sample differs from the original state. If the command, entry point, or permission conditions are changed as well, the run may still be useful as a reference, but it cannot be used to revise this decision.

Here, "current revision" refers to the version point retained at the time of comparison, not necessarily the latest available version, nor does it mean that any cache entry should be pinned to that point. The "cache" in the page title retains the name used in the discussion at the time; this decision provides no implementation rules for cache invalidation, writes, or cleanup.

## Approaches Considered at the Time

| Approach | What it could provide at the time | Why it was not adopted or not adopted more broadly |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retain the current revision and continue examining the original state | Could preserve the relationship between the existing failure sample and the original entry point | The original command parameters are missing, so the existing records alone do not allow direct reproduction |
| Rebuild the environment to reproduce the issue | Could provide a new runtime environment | There is no way to confirm whether the new environment still corresponds to the original state, and rebuilding would obscure the conditions that were originally missing |
| Hold the entry point and command fixed, replacing only the current revision | Could produce a single-variable comparison | The account with standard permissions had not yet been enabled, blocking the run; the comparison cannot be passed off as a completed validation |
| First split out `response selector` | Could allow the two failure exit paths to be examined separately | The current callers of `editor state` have not been confirmed, so neither the scope of the split nor the scope of a rollback can yet be finalized |

The first option is the decision on this page. The third is a form of experiment subsequently allowed as follow-up, not a reversal of the first option. The fourth remains an interface-level direction to be checked; it has not received authorization to "rebuild the environment."

## Changes Brought About by the Missing Parameters

ATCA-011 initially recorded only the fact that the original command in the trade-off record was missing parameters. Work then began to recover the complete command, but the entry-point hint on the page was not updated in step; the action due at the deadline was also no longer valid. Three things need to be distinguished here: parameters really were missing in the original state, someone later tried to recover them, and the page still directed people to an expired entry point. The latter two do not supply the missing values for the first.

Therefore, this decision does not backfill the old state with parameters that might later be recovered. If the complete command is ultimately confirmed, it should be attached alongside the original record as a new addendum, explicitly stating which gap it fills. If the parameters come from another run record, their relationship to the old entry point, the current revision, and the failure sample should also be explained first, rather than merging them merely because the names match.

This is also a practical reason for not choosing to rebuild the environment. Missing parameters are not evidence that the environment itself is damaged. Rebuilding outright would change many unrecorded conditions at once, so even if the output differed in the end, it would be impossible to determine whether the change came from the parameters, entry point, revision, or new environment. Preserving the original state at least avoids conflating these issues into a single conclusion.

## Record of the Single-Variable Rerun

ATCA-015 recorded a comparison rerun: the Quality Signal Dashboard was already able to reproduce the relevant behavior, but execution was blocked because the account with standard permissions had not yet been enabled. This status only shows that the attempt reached the permissions boundary; it does not show that the current revision has passed, nor that the original state is no longer valid.

The card also recorded a detail that could easily mislead later readers: the on-call reply addressed the previous entry, not this card. Accordingly, that reply is neither a run result for this decision nor evidence that the permissions issue has been resolved. Attaching a reply from an adjacent record to this card would conflate the three statuses "reproduced," "blocked," and "handled."

For any subsequent comparisons, retain these minimum identifying details: the elements-core-quality-signal used, the current entry point, whether the missing parts of the original command have been filled in, which revision was replaced, and whether the account with the required permissions meets the conditions for running. Not every item needs to be restated on this page; they should appear with the specific run record. The only requirement here is: if any one of them is missing, the result cannot supersede the original state.

## Handling the Earlier Proposed Split

The earlier version favored splitting `response selector` out separately from alongside `variable metadata`. That preference remains, but starting with this round, it will no longer be described as a settled remediation path. The reason is simple: it came from observing differences between the failure exit paths, not from a complete list of callers.

The current callers of `editor state` remain unresolved. Until that gap is filled, it is impossible to determine whether the split affects only the Quality Signal Dashboard itself, or whether a rollback should restore the old entry point or an earlier structure. The earlier question of "whether a rollback should only restore the old entry point" therefore remains open.

This does not require stopping the examination of `response selector`. It can be the subject of local inspection and comparison, but the findings should not be packaged as a reason to rebuild the environment. If it is later found to be unrelated to the old state, the earlier draft's proposed split should be marked as not applicable in an addendum, rather than quietly rewritten as though it had been ruled out from the outset.

## Objections and Trade-offs

The objection to rebuilding the environment is not that rebuilding has no value, but that, given the current material, it cannot serve the role of "restoring the original state." Those supporting a rebuild want to move past the missing parameters and expired hints as quickly as possible; that motivation is reasonable, but it addresses obtaining runnable conditions, not restoring the meaning of the old record.

The costs of retaining the current revision are also clear: it will not restore the parameters on its own, update the entry-point hint on the page, or make the not-yet-enabled account with standard permissions usable. The decision accepts these unfinished items in exchange for keeping the original and new samples from being conflated in the records. Conditions still to be supplied belong in subsequent run records; this page only fixes the relationship between the two.

Another objection is that the sample may be too narrow. That objection is valid, so the decision has not been generalized to the shared main product, unknown callers, or other projects. The Quality Signal Dashboard's own failure samples can support local trade-offs, but they do not imply that external entry points should also retain the same revision or use the same rebuilding approach.

## Reversal and Addenda

The trigger for reversing this decision is not "another failure." What is needed is material capable of changing the basis of comparison: for example, the complete original command is confirmed and can be matched to the old state item by item; or an explainable difference is obtained with the current entry point and command held fixed and only the current revision replaced; or the originally retained revision is confirmed not to correspond to the failure sample under discussion. In these cases, the old entry point should be restored as the starting point for comparison, and a new trade-off record should be opened, rather than rewriting this page so that new facts appear to have been part of the old decision.

Enabling access, correcting expired entry-point hints, and recovering parameters can all become supplementary material, but each addresses only its own gap. A run record obtained after access is enabled cannot substitute for the command's provenance; updating an entry-point hint cannot prove that the old state is reproducible; recovering the command also does not automatically establish the callers of `editor state`. These boundaries preserve the meaning of different records, rather than delaying subsequent work.

Relevant leads are in ATCA-011 and ATCA-015. The project's entry point for the decision draft is `docs/adj-elements-core/decisions/elements-core-quality-signal-cache-vs-original-state-tradeoff.md`. DOC-28 contains an on-call record of a failed run; it can help pinpoint the behavior at the time, but it does not change this page's trade-off between preserving the original state and performing comparison reruns.

Finally, the wording of the earlier version is retained: do not rebuild the environment for the current revision. It should now be understood within the limits set on this page—the original state remains preserved; controlled comparisons can be performed separately; the records of missing parameters, a permissions block, and a reply mistakenly sent to the previous entry still do not constitute grounds for replacing the original state.

# Documentation Site Entry Migration Index

The index file is located at `docs/adj-elements-dev-portal/migration/current-entry-old-entry-migration-index.md`. Here, an entry is a location in docs or guide that directs users to documentation, release notes, or legacy content; it is not determined by whether a file with the same name appears in the directory. Record the old entry and replacement location separately, so that documentation updates make clear which link was actually replaced.

Do not merge the two records both called "current entry" yet. Treat them as the same migration only when both the source and the callers still using them match; if one comes from docs and the other from guide, retain each one's old entry, replacement location, and adopters, even if they ultimately lead to similar content. If the callers cannot currently be located, leave the original documentation marked as outdated; do not record speculation as a completed migration.

Perform the migration in the following order:

1. Trace the old entry to the content it actually points to, record the replacement location, and retain the docs or guide location containing the old entry.
2. Update each caller confirmed to still be in use so that it uses the replacement location. Update callers first, then release notes; the new entry appearing in the directory does not mean the switch is complete.
3. Release notes record only entry changes that have actually been implemented. Outdated content that needs to be retained may remain where it is; make clear that it documents the old entry, and do not treat it as evidence that the new location has been adopted.
4. Recheck the sources and adopters of same-named entries. The two records must not overwrite each other merely because their names match; the index should show the replacement location corresponding to each old link.

Previously, failure paths near the same entry were recorded together. That is insufficient for restoration: links from different sources may need to return to different old locations. # Postmortem: Two Documentation-Site Records Were Not Merged

The same user-facing entry point on the documentation site once contained two revisions at the same time, and both appeared as the current revision. The entry point did not distinguish the older record from the later one. People viewing the version notes could only see the content side by side and could not determine from the entry point itself which section corresponded to the material that was still in use at the time. This record addresses the issue of two versions of the material not being merged; it was not an incident in which the documentation site as a whole was unavailable.

The earliest field assessment was based on fallback reason. It differed from the explanation in the older record and initially looked like an exception left by the old content in the new entry point. After further checking, that assessment did not hold up sufficiently: each record retained its own context; they had simply been placed in the same entry point. The difference in fallback reason can show that the two records were not identical, but by itself cannot show which one should supersede the other.

## Changes Observed

- At first inspection, the entry point was already displaying two revisions at the same time. The older record was still visible but was not marked as an older version; the newer record had no separate boundary either.
- The subsequent check preserved the page version as it was at the time and did not continue retrying in the hope that the entry point would become a single version on its own. Retries would not fill in the missing relationship between the two records; instead, they might cause the last display to be mistaken for a recovery result.
- During review, tracing back through the original input confirmed only the current entry point. The reviewer did not reproduce any other branch, so those branches cannot be used to fill in the cause or impact scope.
- The current entry point still showed `model icon`. This was only a detail visible on the page at the time and is not enough to prove which adopters used either version.

Here, "not merged" is easily understood as needing to combine the two pieces of text into one. That was not what happened in the field. Both the content and the order in which the two revisions appeared should be preserved; the problem was that the entry point presented them side by side as the same current state. If the newer record were to directly overwrite the older one, the context in which the old assessment was formed would be lost; if only the older record were kept, the later finding would again be placed in the current position. The records need to be distinguishable by version before discussing whether their content is still worth retaining.

## Impact Assessment

The impact was on version identification at the user-facing entry point. People reading content on the documentation site might treat the old assessment as the current explanation, or, because the two passages appeared side by side, mistakenly assume they described the same change. The available field record contains no adoption scope, so the impact cannot be expanded to all users of the documentation site, nor can this be used to infer that other entry points had the same mix-up.

The difference in fallback reason that was initially observed was briefly treated as an investigation path; attribution was not pursued along it afterward. It appeared at the same time as the mixing of the two records, but there is no evidence that it caused the entry-point state to change. This correction remains in the record so that later readers who see only the first paragraph do not misread an inconsistent explanation as a confirmed root cause.

## Handling at the Time

The version in `docs/adj-elements-dev-portal/incidents/elements-dev-portal-documentation-portal-two-version-records-not-merged.md` was retained at the time, and further retries were stopped. The stopping point was not because the two versions of the material had already been organized, but because no branch outside the current entry point had been reproduced, and continuing would not add any facts that could be confirmed.

The purpose of retaining the older version was also not to reinstate it as the current explanation. The older record documents the earlier assessment, and the later record documents what was seen afterward; both need to remain in their respective revision contexts. The entry-point anomaly should be described as "the version boundary was not displayed," rather than written as saying that the old material had been deleted, replaced, or proven invalid.

## Remaining Gaps

The specific time when the mixing first appeared was not recorded; the time blank in the field record still needs to be filled from changes to the documentation site from that period. Adoption scope also remains unconfirmed: at present, the only thing that can be confirmed is that the current entry point displayed the two versions side by side; it cannot be confirmed which users, documentation pages, or version descriptions actually read either version.

Another unresolved item is why fallback reason differed from the older record. It can serve as a comparison point in later cross-checking, but not as an attribution for this incident. The branches not reproduced during review remain pending investigation; do not connect them to this timeline until new page records are available.
