# Dependency Boundary Entry Migration Index

The index still covers license-related dependency sources, adoption scope, and exit responsibility. It is not a dependency list: each record must at minimum show the old entry point, replacement location, callers currently using it, and who owns the exit decision. If no caller can be found, the old record remains in the index; do not use a similarly named alternate path to make it appear complete.

Early on, the split between `model icon` and `group identity` was treated as the primary basis for judgment. That assessment can now be retained only as a historical note. The two failure exits are different, which indicates that the entry points should not be conflated; but that alone cannot prove that a particular adopter has migrated, nor can it replace actual read results.

## What to Leave Before Migration

After locating the old entry to process through `docs/adj-elements/migration/current-entry-old-entry-migration-index.md`, first add a line recording the state at the original location: who the adopter is, what current revision was observed, and what the last position that could be confirmed before failure was. ATCC-002 requires the current revision to remain unknown until it has been confirmed that collection or execution actually occurred. Do not enter an inferred value in the index just to make a row look complete.

The backfill direction for ATCC-005 is the reverse: work back one slot from the current entry and record the last state that could be confirmed before failure. It can coexist with "current revision unconfirmed"; the former is an old state that was observed, while the latter is a new state that must not replace it. Do not merge the two columns.

The minimum record format used at the time was:

```text
Old entry point: ________
Replacement location: ________
Adopter: ________
Last confirmed state before failure: ________
Current revision: Confirmed / Unconfirmed
Second read or run: ________
Exit responsibility: ________
```

Blank fields are not cosmetic fill-ins. In particular, if no result was recorded for the second read or run, do not substitute the final state. The guidance in ATCC-012 is specifically for this kind of gap: if only the final state remains, leave the field blank.

## Limited-Scope Replacement

Switch only one known adopter to the replacement location at a time. Keep the old entry until that adopter's first result can be compared against what was obtained at the original location. This comparison is limited to the content directly obtained by the same consumer before and after migration; do not use reworked summaries or screenshots to fill in the original result.

```text
Old entry point ──> Adopter A ──> Original result
   │
   └── Retain

Replacement location ──> Adopter A ──> First result
                    │
                    └── Second read or run
```

When the first difference appears, mark in the index which entry point or read stage it occurs at, then stop expanding this migration batch. The verification method in ATCC-009 likewise traces the original entry to a real consumer and stops at the first difference; it is not a search for a final page that "looks normal."

An earlier version said, "Once the replacement location was readable, it was possible to prepare to stop maintaining the old path." This statement no longer applies. Readability only shows that the replacement location exists; it does not mean that the adopter's read, the current revision, and one subsequent result have all been recorded. This sentence is retained to explain why a decommissioning marker once appeared in the old index prematurely.

## Rollback

When the first result differs, or when the second read or run yields no result, do not continue moving that adopter to the replacement location. Restore the old entry's reachability, retain the recorded replacement location and difference description, and then re-examine the original input once. Rollback does not mean deleting this trial-migration row; the exit responsibility must remain because the old entry may still have other adopters.

Once the interface confirmation is received, modify only the corresponding fields. The record under ATCC-006 was once found to have the date for "Execution record" earlier than the date for "Current result"; later, only the "Execution record" and "Current result" entries were reordered, and the event date was not changed. The index was therefore reordered according to the actual order in which events occurred; the date was not changed to make the sequence look coherent.

No current caller for `direction-safe suffix` has been found yet. This item remains marked as not yet rechecked.

# Dependency Boundary Entry Point Migration Index

This index was initially treated as an appendix to an entry point cleanup. Some old rows listed only a replacement location, while others contained only a consumer name; the two kinds of records were later mixed together, making it read as though the same batch of migrations had already been completed. Those rows are still retained because they show where the early assessments came from, and because some old entry points are still referenced.

The scope of the index has not expanded: the dependency sources, adoption scope, and retirement responsibilities associated with license are recorded separately under `elements-supply-boundary`. This index does not include pages with similar names, nor does it incorporate records from peripheral projects. Only the old entry points, replacement locations, and callers still using them can be confirmed; the item that cannot be rechecked retains its old status.

## Earliest Notes on the Split

The first version framed the issue as a comparison between two ways of categorizing it: continue with `model icon`, or split out `group identity` on its own. At the time, the two sections were seen to have different exits after failure, so the latter was favored. That preference remains in the index, but it should no longer be treated as evidence that the migration is complete.

The diagram from that time is also retained below. It represents a reversible trial migration, not the final topology:

```text
Old entry point ── Retain ──> Existing consumers
  │
  └── Trial migration ──> Replacement location
                 │
                 └── Return to the old entry point if inconsistent
```

The "different exits" in the old note only explain why the two locations should not be described in the same row. The note did not answer whether consumers had actually changed their read location, nor whether the old entry point could be retired. During later reviews of the index, this was the step most easily misread: treating a split in categorization as a replacement in actual calls.

There were also two blank items at the time. No current caller had been found for `direction-safe suffix`; nor had it been settled whether rollback should restore only the old entry point. Neither issue disappeared on its own when replacement locations were added later. The former has still not been rechecked, while the latter received more specific handling in later small-scale trial migrations, but that handling should not be written retroactively into the first version's conclusions.

## What a Row in the Index Represents

A row for an old entry point is more than just a directory link. It relates to at least four different things: where the dependency source enters, which adoption scope is still reading from it, what the replacement location is intended to take over, and who retains or retires that relationship. Early records often covered only one or two of these, so "there is a new location" does not mean "the old location can be deleted".

The current practice is to add details in the original file: `docs/adj-elements/migration/current-entry-old-entry-migration-index.md`. Find the old entry point first, rather than inferring the original state from the replacement location. Then record the consumers that can be confirmed near that same row, so that the same name appearing in different paragraphs is not mistaken for different users. The replacement location must also be retained alongside the old entry point; it is the destination for a trial migration, not a label that replaces the historical record.

The recommended record format is shown below. It is a working format added later, and cannot be used to prove that every early row already contained these details:

```text
Old entry point: ________
Replacement location: ________
Consumer: ________
Dependency source: ________
Adoption scope: ________
Last confirmed state before failure: ________
Current revision: Confirmed / Unconfirmed
First read or run: ________
Second read or run: ________
Retirement responsibility: ________
```

"Current revision" and "last confirmed state before failure" must be kept separate. ATCC-002 require the current revision to remain unknown until collection or execution is confirmed to have actually taken place. That unknown must not be filled in with the "last observed state". The latter is the old location that could be confirmed before the failure, and ATCC-005 require backfilling one slot before the current entry point to preserve it; it cannot replace an unconfirmed new result.

This distinction arose from a very ordinary misreading of the index: someone saw only that the old entry point still had a last state, and marked the current revision as confirmed as well. As a result, it was later impossible to tell whether a read had taken place or whether only the content from before the failure had been retained. Since then, the index has kept two fields, without merging them even when one is blank.

## Trial Migration Batch Boundaries

A replacement location cannot take over all consumers in the index at once. Select only one known consumer per batch, and keep the old entry point readable. The reason is not to prolong the migration, but that the old records already lack consistent result evidence; after changing multiple consumers at once, even if a difference appears, the index cannot show whether it comes from the entry point, the consumer, or the order in which details were added.

A trial migration uses before-and-after reads by the same consumer for comparison. First retain the first result available at the original location, then have that consumer read from the replacement location, and finally add the second read or run. Compare the raw, direct results, not conclusive descriptions excerpted from pages. The relationships available in the index are as follows:

```text
Old entry point ──> Consumer A ──> First result
   │
   └── Retain until the batch ends

Replacement location ──> Consumer A ──> First result after migration
                    │
                    └── Second read or run
```

ATCC-009 narrow the verification further: find an actual consumer and have them read through the original entry point to the current revision, stopping at the first difference. This stopping point is important. The index is not looking for a state that looks consistent in the end; the first difference is where the decision is made on whether the batch should continue. If the difference occurs between the old entry point and the replacement location, it must not be skipped in order to fill in subsequent fields.

An "actual consumer" also cannot be replaced by a name mentioned in the directory. An early row treated the appearance of a new entry point as a consumer migration, but a later review found that only the person on duty had been confirmed, not the current version. This issue appeared in the records for ATCC-002: for the last consumer, the person on duty was confirmed, but the current revision was not. Therefore, the consumer field and the current revision field must still be kept separately; the former answers who was present, while the latter answers whether the version read was the one claimed.

## When the Second Result Is Missing

The second read or run is not an optional note. ATCC-012 specifically recorded the case where "the second result for the current revision is missing": when only the final state remains, the index is still left blank. That blank is more useful than an assumed success state, because it tells whoever takes over later that the comparison was interrupted after the first result.

An old version stated, "Once the replacement location is readable, there is no need to continue maintaining the old path". This assessment is obsolete. Readability only shows that the replacement location can be found; it does not prove that both the first and second results have been obtained for the same consumer, nor that the current revision has been confirmed. The original assessment is retained to provide traceable context for the old decommissioning markers; it should not be used to move new batches forward.

If the second result is missing, the handling order is:

1. Retain parallel records of the old entry point and the replacement location;
2. Mark the first result already obtained in this batch, without copying the final state into the second-result field;
3. Do not extend the same replacement location to any other consumers;
4. Restore the conditions under which this consumer can use the old entry point;
5. Read again from the same input, and update the row only when new direct results are available.

Restoration here does not mean deleting the trial migration. Deleting it would obscure why the replacement location was tried, and would also lose the fact that retirement responsibility remains unresolved. The old entry point may have other adoption scopes, and restoring one consumer does not mean reapproving all old paths.

## The Earlier Issue with Date Ordering

After the interface confirmation in ATCC-006, the index once showed the date of the "execution record" as earlier than that of the "current result". The event dates were not changed at the time; only the execution record and the current result were reordered chronologically. This revision preserved two facts: records may be added later than the events, and reading order should not overwrite the original occurrence times for convenience.

Therefore, if a result is seen first in a migration row and the execution record is added later, mark it as a later addition, rather than disguising the date it was added as the execution time. Conversely, if execution has been recorded but the current revision has not yet been confirmed, do not mark it as confirmed merely to make the sequence look tidy. The purpose of the index is to preserve the relationships that could be traced during migration, not to rewrite a gap-free account of the process.

After interface confirmation, update only the corresponding fields. The handling in ATCC-006 was a single-item update: after confirmation of the maintenance entry point was received, the records near that entry point were updated, while the other `adj-elements` rows retained their original status. This approach prevents a single reply from being expanded into a migration conclusion for the entire table.

## Criteria for Retiring an Old Entry Point

Before an old entry point is retired, the index should at least show the replacement location, the callers still using it, and retirement responsibility. For each consumer preparing to stop using the old entry point, first confirm that its current revision is no longer unknown, then retain one direct read result; if the index lacks the second result, continue to treat it as incomplete. Earlier versions listed "the replacement location exists" and "historical queries are still available" as conditions for stopping maintenance of the old path. This statement was overly optimistic, and is now retained as part of the old process rather than used on its own.

Retirement responsibility is not a name field for the person who removes the entry point from the directory. It identifies who needs to confirm that the adoption scope no longer depends on the old entry point, and who decides to restore it when a difference appears. If the index can confirm only the replacement location, but not the consumer, do not mark it as "retirement complete". If only the consumer can be confirmed but the current revision is unconfirmed, it likewise cannot be closed out.

For old records that still cannot be rechecked, the safest status is to retain a note that they are outdated. They may still provide a starting point for later reads; changing them to "unused" would lose the boundaries that had not yet been confirmed at the time.

## Old Statements Still in the Index

- "Judge migration by the appearance of a new entry point in the directory." Obsolete. The appearance of a new entry point does not mean consumers have switched to it.
- "Once `group identity` is split out, the old path can be taken offline." Obsolete. The split is a categorization decision, not confirmation of calls.
- "If the second result was not retained, fill it in with the final state." Obsolete. The blank items associated with ATCC-012 should remain blank.
- "Correct all dates to match the reading order." Obsolete. Execution records and current results may be reordered, but event dates must not be rewritten.

These old statements have not been erased from historical versions because the index has long been used as a navigation entry point. When reading an old row, first check whether it is subject to the restrictions above, then decide whether it can be used to plan the next migration batch.

## Where to Start When Taking Over

Start with the old entry point row in `docs/adj-elements/migration/current-entry-old-entry-migration-index.md`, rather than the summary of replacement locations. First identify whether the row still belongs to `elements-supply-boundary`, then check whether the consumer, current revision, and second result all have explicit contents. Whatever is missing should remain a gap; do not substitute records from similar pages.

ATCC-002, ATCC-005, ATCC-006, ATCC-009 and ATCC-012 should be used only when reviewing how their respective individual items were handled. The index itself continues to preserve the migration relationships among old entry points, replacement locations, and consumers. DOC-38 can be used to look up the current maintenance entry point for `elements-supply-boundary`; it does not replace the trial migration, rollback, and outdated rows retained here.

The current callers for `direction-safe suffix` have still not been added to the index. Without a reliable consumer, this item should not enter the next replacement batch.

# Postmortem: Two Dependency-Boundary Record Versions Were Not Merged

What we saw this time was not a single missing record, but the current revision of two revisions being placed under the same entry point. The entry point could still be opened, so it was initially treated as an ordinary display difference; only when we compared it with the old record did we find that the group identity was already different, while readers had no way to determine which version they were seeing.

## Observed Behavior

Two sets of content remain under the same entry point. The current revision shown on the page appears continuous, but its corresponding group identity does not match the old record. The most direct impact is that judgments about the dependency source and license will be carried over to the other set of records; the scope of adoption will become unclear as well. There is no evidence that the two sets of records have been merged; the only thing we can establish is that the entry point did not keep them separate.

## What Happened

- On the first comparison, we only recorded that the group identity differed from the old record and suspected a grouping change during import.
- We then checked the entry point and found that both revisions had been written as the current revision; at the time, we still thought keeping the newer one would be enough.
- After reopening the old material, we did not continue overwriting the original file; instead, we left the version from that point in `docs/adj-elements/incidents/elements-dependency-boundary-audit-two-version-records-not-merged.md`.
- Further retries were stopped. The existing direction-safe suffix could be restored, so we attributed the issue at the time to the entry-point suffix not keeping up, rather than to the record itself not being merged.

This attribution was not reliable in hindsight, but the assessment of the old entry point remains recorded here: it held that restoring the suffix would put the two revisions back in their respective positions. The available material does not show that this applies to all adopters, nor that it explains the change in group identity.

## Impact and Remaining Gaps

Those affected are people who check dependency boundaries through this entry point. If they directly use the current revision shown at the entry point, they may mistake the old record for a continuation of the same group; if they look only at group identity, they may mistakenly think the old record has been replaced. Neither interpretation was resolved in the materials.

The reason for the tablet breakpoint change was not found at the time. The missing point in time is still: ____. Another unresolved point is why response selector was recorded as the landing point; no basis suitable for inclusion in this record was found to determine whether it is related to the two revisions sharing an entry point.

The attachments are still maintained by the elements · Dependency Boundary Audit knowledge base. This file preserves the assessment made when retries were stopped; it does not fold any entry-point changes that may have occurred later back into this account of events.

# Compatibility Catalog Failed-Run Procedure

This page preserves the on-call sequence for the failed run demo-compatibility-catalog. It was later used to handle similar catalog issues, but originally covered just one run. A recovered page or a green result cannot replace the failure window left by that run.

The old draft listed `request header` as the first entry point, treated `upload capability` as a marker to leave the incident state intact, and stopped when `callback section` was missing. These three items remain in the previous version as a reference for what was observed at the time; they are not stages that necessarily appear in every later run. Later notes shifted the focus back to the original input, the page timeline, and the first record after recovery.

## Preserve the incident state first

Open `docs/adj-demo/runbooks/demo-compatibility-catalog-failed-run-on-call-page.md`. This is the existing handover file for demo · Compatibility Catalog. Find the matching run there first; do not start a separate record under a similar name in another project.

Before any refresh, restart, permission change, or data regeneration, record three things: the original input, the current revision observed this time, and the first visible page result. You may also save the version of `server template` from that moment, but it is only an attachment to the incident record; its absence should not prevent you from recording the first difference. Only refresh or recreate when that action is itself a step to be verified.

The value eventually displayed on the page is only supporting evidence. The anomaly recorded in ATCD-003 was a mismatch between the current revision and the page timeline, so first arrange the records in their original order of occurrence, then put the final page value after them. Do not rewrite an earlier empty result as though it never happened just because the last screen looked normal.

## Stop and assess at the first difference

Compare against the most recent successful sample. Change only one condition per comparison. If no successful sample was saved, do not change the input, version, and page state all at once to manufacture a "comparison result." Record what differs and whether it appeared before catalog generation, during page rendering, or only after recovery.

If the difference is still within the scope of demo · Compatibility Catalog itself, retain the original input and the first difference, then continue to the next step. If the difference involves public contracts, migration records, or caller compatibility related to openapi and api, stop at that difference and hand the entry point and observed behavior to the public interface owner. Keep the user-side incident state in the demo project; do not mix user-visible content into the interface assessment.

The old version suggested, "If the incident state is inconsistent, contact the maintainer." That is too broad; when taking over, first establish a stopping point. If any of the original input, current revision, or first result is missing, do not assume the catalog was generated successfully or treat the default page as a successful sample.

## Zero-result branch

When the page returns no result, first check the entry point in use and the original current revision. The records in ATCD-005 require checking both: if both are missing, leave the status unknown rather than filling the gaps with later summaries or the recovered page. If only one is missing, attach the one you can find alongside the failure window and explicitly state that the other was not obtained.

Do not rerun the same request at this point to "verify zero results." A rerun creates a new page timeline and cannot establish what happened in the first run. If further verification is necessary, record it separately as the next run, and retain the conclusion that this run stopped with zero results.

The toolchain was pinned in one later note. That restriction was a condition of that part of the on-call record; it does not mean every catalog run must switch to or pin the same toolchain. If the incident state depends on it, document that before continuing. Do not silently change it and then splice the results back into the old record.

## Handling a recovered run

Recovery only means the catalog can return results again; it does not mean the first failure has been explained. ATCD-008 require appending the recovery result alongside the original incident state without overwriting the original failure window or object. Keep the input, version, and page sequence saved before recovery, even if the results seen later are more complete.

Starting at the recovery point, capture only the first current revision. ATCD-010 point to this step: do not put later summaries, repeat runs, or manually curated pages under "first record after recovery." If the first record is still empty, still inconsistent with the page, or was not obtained at all, record that as it is and stop; do not wait for the next round of results to close it out.

If the recovery action itself changed permissions, input, or data, record when that action occurred relative to the original incident state, but do not backfill the state before the first failure with the post-recovery state. Keep the original failure and recovery result side by side so later readers can see that they are not the same page state.

## Handover entry

The handover entry only needs enough for the next shift to continue this run: the file entry point, whether the original input has been retained, whether the current revision has been obtained, the step where the first difference or zero result occurred, whether recovery was performed, and whether the first record after recovery was captured. Rejected hypotheses can be noted alongside the entry, but do not present a hypothesis as the cause.

This page still retains the old wording `request header`, `upload capability`, and `callback section` because it belongs to the field notes for that run. When taking over a new failure, preserve the material at the stopping points defined here. The old answer said, "If the entry point exists, caller replay can be considered done." That no longer applies. # Component Release Cadence Decision Record

The initial draft recorded only the conclusions, and a subsequent review found that the debate at the time could easily be reduced to the single phrase "whether to change the window". That wording obscured the real distinction: the existing entry point can serve as the starting point for checks, but that does not mean it is already sufficient to establish what users will see; conversely, even a plausible explanation of the implementation cannot go into the release summary without reproduced output.

This addendum does not turn unconfirmed points into definite conclusions. It clearly separates the scope finalized in this round, the approaches not adopted, and the objections that still need to remain on record. The release cadence discussion remains centered on the public calls of the existing Elements package and reproducible output, rather than being determined by any single source-code location.

## Outcome of This Round

1. The current oas-transform entry point remains the starting point for this round of release checks.
2. The release window will not be adjusted based on judgments that lack reproduced output.
3. The release summary will record only conclusions within the scope covered by the reproduced output already available.
4. Speculation about implementation causes may remain in the review materials, but must not be recast as user observations, much less used to expand the approved scope.

These items are different aspects of the same decision. Retaining the entry point lets checks begin with existing public calls; leaving the window unchanged reflects that the available materials do not support a larger cadence change; restricting the summary prevents future readers of the release information from mistaking a provisional explanation for a verified fact.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Public calls in the Elements package] --> B[Reproducible output]
  B --> C[User observations]
  C --> D[Conclusions in the release summary]
  A --> E[Implementation speculation]
  E --> F[Retained in the review record]
```

The two paths in the diagram do not mean that implementation speculation has no value. They simply show that the two have different thresholds for inclusion in release materials: public calls and output can support judgments about externally visible behavior; interfaces, call names, or internal paths usually only help propose or narrow down an explanation.

## Judgments Carried Over from the Initial Draft

The initial working assumption was that, since the current oas-transform entry point was still the known starting point for checks, the release cadence could remain unchanged with that entry point as its basis. The counterexample added during the review was simple: the existence of an entry point only tells us where to start looking, not that all behavior beyond that entry point has been reproduced. Combining the two would make the release summary turn "can be located" into "has been proven".

Accordingly, in this version, "retain the current entry point" from the initial draft is limited to the boundary of the checks, rather than a promise of stability. This change in wording matters. It neither denies the role of the entry point nor declares that the window must be changed immediately; it rejects using the entry point itself as a substitute for output.

During the review, we traced back through the interface, oas, and elements call names in `packages/elements/src/utils/oas/types.ts`. That trail is useful for confirming what the discussion at the time referred to, and can also help avoid mixing in adjacent components. But declarations in the file are not evidence for the release cadence. If the httpOperation call relationships need to be traced further, DOC-01 is where the materials for that limited scope are retained; this record keeps only the choices made in this review.

## The Two Options Do Not Have the Same Prerequisites

**Retain the current oas-transform entry point.** This option was adopted not because it is inherently safer than adjusting the window, but because it provides a known, traceable starting point. From here, the review examines public calls and then uses reproducible output to determine which statements can go into the summary. This keeps release checks within the scope covered by existing materials, without requiring the shape of the interface to be extrapolated into a complete behavioral model.

The trade-off is that the cadence will not change immediately in response to an explanation that has yet to be verified. Some may see this as overly conservative, but this round did not treat "adjust as soon as possible" as a separate objective. If an adjustment depends on a user-visible change, that change must first be demonstrated; if all that can be demonstrated is a suspicion about the implementation, it remains only a suspicion. Retaining the entry point does not rule out later adjustments; it simply rules out writing down a conclusion in favor of an adjustment first and then looking for output.

**Adjust the release window.** This option remained a candidate during the review but did not become the decision for this round. Adjusting the window means that the summary and subsequent release judgments would take on a broader scope; what it requires is not the statement "the existing entry point may not be enough", but output that is reproducible and sufficient to establish user observations. The requirement in the meeting materials was direct: conclusions without reproduced output are not to go into the release summary for now.

Not adopting a window adjustment does not declare that the window must never change, nor does it mean that all objections are wrong. What is rejected here is a sequence: first move the window based on implementation speculation, then package that speculation as an established fact. That sequence would leave readers unable to tell whether the output pointed to a problem or we merely inferred a problem from the call path.

## How to Read the Materials During Review

The order followed in the review is not intended to turn the review into a lengthy process, but to avoid making any piece of material carry implications it cannot support.

First, look at the public calls in the existing Elements package. Public calls establish the entry point for the discussion and the scope of what is being examined. They show where checks should begin and help exclude unrelated components; they do not automatically show that every result following a call has been observed.

Next, look at reproducible output. The output determines whether a statement can be included in the release summary. Here, "reproducible" does not mean that someone has seen a phenomenon before, but that the same judgment can be supported by results that can be obtained repeatedly. Without that basis, the summary can only say that verification is still in progress, not fill in the causal chain for the reader.

Then separate user observations from implementation speculation. User observations are behaviors that public calls and output can directly support; implementation speculation consists of explanations formed from interfaces, call paths, or other internal clues. Both can remain in the review materials at the same time, but they must be written differently. The former can become release conclusions within a limited scope, while the latter must explicitly remain candidate explanations.

Only then decide whether to expand the scope. Scope is not determined by how heated the discussion is, nor can it be expanded just because the entry point's name appears to cover a broad range. Approving only the parts covered by existing evidence both prevents the summary from growing ever broader and allows the next review to clearly identify which part is new material rather than a reinterpretation of old sentences.

This approach to reading the materials also explains why the interface in `types.ts` cannot be treated as sufficient grounds for adjusting the window. It helps identify the subject, but does not directly provide user observations; likewise, a public call can be a starting point for reproduction, but cannot replace reproduction itself when no output is available yet.

## Writing the Release Summary

The summary should retain conclusions that can be used for release judgments, rather than importing the entire review debate. For the materials in this round, the following belong in the summary: the scope of public calls to which a conclusion applies, the reproduced output supporting that conclusion, and adjacent areas the conclusion does not cover. This lets readers know both what the information says and what it does not say.

Two types of content should stay out of the summary. The first is judgments based only on an implementation explanation, without supporting output. They may help locate issues in the next round, but should not masquerade as user-visible phenomena that have already occurred. The second is global assertions extrapolated from output for a limited scope. Even if the local results are valid, it must not therefore be assumed that the entire Elements package, all entry points, or subsequent windows have undergone the same verification.

The summary need not repeatedly state that "the current entry point is retained". This is a review decision, not a prefix for every piece of release information. What actually needs to be recorded is the scope of public calls within which a conclusion holds and whether it has reproduced output. This preserves the information needed to judge the cadence without mixing implementation paths and release conclusions into a single paragraph.

## Reservations Still on Record

The first reservation is that there is still a gap between the entry point and the scope. The current oas-transform entry point is sufficient as the place to begin checks in this round, but no materials justify describing it as representative of all related behavior. If output emerges later that affects only an adjacent area, it must not be forced into the existing conclusion; first determine whether it still falls within the scope approved by this decision.

The second reservation is that output and explanation may temporarily be inconsistent. Output describes the observed results, while implementation speculation describes the causes. When the two do not align, the release summary gives priority to preserving the output and its scope of applicability, without making a premature ruling on the causes. The causes can continue to be discussed, but they should not override the observed boundaries merely because they are easier to explain.

The third reservation is that adjusting the window has not been permanently rejected. It simply was not approved based on the materials in this round. Keeping it in the decision record prevents the next discussion from mistakenly assuming that "an adjustment was never considered", and also prevents this round's deferral from being misread as long-term policy. If an adjustment is proposed again next time, it should start with new public calls and reproduced output, rather than extracting an isolated statement of preference from this record.

## Conditions for Reopening the Discussion

The emergence of new reproduced output does not automatically revise this round's decision. First check whether the output corresponds to a subject that can be confirmed through public calls, then determine whether it supports a user observation or an implementation hypothesis; only the former can support expanding the scope of the summary or reopening discussion of the window. If the output only adds support within the existing scope, the entry point can continue to serve as the starting point for checks, without broadening the cadence discussion into a complete reset.

Until then, the current decision stands: retain the entry point, do not adjust the window based on judgments without reproduced output, and do not admit conclusions into the release summary that extend beyond the coverage of the existing output. The options not adopted and the reservations remain on file for comparison in subsequent reviews.
